library(ggplot2)

This document is reference material for the deterministic functions that are used in this
book and for several others that are common in ecology. For each function it gives the
formula, its properties, R code and a description of when the function is useful.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd) explains the tools with which the properties are
derived (limits, derivatives and special points), so the entries apply these tools without
explaining them again.

Every entry has the same parts: a summary of the function, a description of when it is
useful and of where it comes from, its formula with the derivation of its landmarks, an
example that is calculated by hand and verified in R, a figure and a practice exercise.
The numbers in the examples are hypothetical and were chosen so that the calculations can
be done by hand.

The symbols are those of Chapter 5. The input is $x$ and the output is $y=f(x)$. The
parameters are called $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$: these letters are positions in a formula, and
every entry says what each of them controls and which units it has. Unless an entry says
otherwise, the parameters are positive and $x\ge0$. The R functions use the same letters
as the formulas, including `c` (R keeps functions and other objects apart, so `c()` still
combines values). The papers cited in the entries are listed in @sec-fn-references.

# Choosing a function {#sec-fn-overview}

The table below lists the functions of this supplement by the properties that we can see
in a plot of data: the values of $x$ for which the function is used, how it starts, how it
ends and what happens in between.
[Choosing a function](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-choosing-function) in Chapter 5 explains
how to use these properties to select candidates for a response, and
[Starting values by eye](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-starting-values) how to read values
of the parameters from a plot.

| Function | Formula | Domain | Left end | Right end | Middle |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [Linear](#sec-fn-linear) | $a+bx$ | all $x$ | straight line | straight line | monotonic |
| [Quadratic](#sec-fn-quadratic) | $a+bx+cx^2$ | all $x$ | grows without bound | grows without bound | one maximum or minimum |
| [Threshold](#sec-fn-threshold) | $a$ if $x<c$, $b$ otherwise | all $x$ | flat | flat | one jump |
| [Hockey stick](#sec-fn-hockey-stick) | $ax$ if $x<c$, $ac$ otherwise | all $x$ | straight line | flat | one breakpoint |
| [Piecewise linear](#sec-fn-piecewise-linear) | two lines joined at $c$ | all $x$ | straight line | straight line | one breakpoint |
| [Hyperbolic](#sec-fn-hyperbolic) | $\dfrac{a}{b+x}$ | $x\ge0$ | finite value | tends to 0 | decreasing |
| [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) | $\dfrac{ax}{b+x}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating |
| [Holling type III](#sec-fn-holling3) | $\dfrac{ax^2}{b^2+x^2}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, accelerating | asymptote | sigmoid |
| [Holling type IV](#sec-fn-holling4) | $\dfrac{ax^2}{b+cx+x^2}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, accelerating | asymptote | hump before the asymptote when $c<0$ |
| [Exponential](#sec-fn-exponential) | $ae^{-bx}$ | $x\ge0$ | finite value | tends to 0 | decreasing |
| [Saturating exponential](#sec-fn-monomolecular) | $a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right)$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating |
| [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) | $axe^{-bx}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | tends to 0 | one maximum |
| [Logistic](#sec-fn-logistic) | $\dfrac{a}{1+e^{-b(x-c)}}$ | all $x$ | close to 0, accelerating | asymptote | sigmoid |
| [Gompertz](#sec-fn-gompertz) | $a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | all $x$ | close to 0, accelerating | asymptote | sigmoid, asymmetric |
| [Bell-shaped](#sec-fn-gaussian) | $a\,e^{-(x-c)^2/(2b^2)}$ | all $x$ | tends to 0 | tends to 0 | one maximum, symmetric |
| [Power law](#sec-fn-power) | $ax^b$ | $x>0$ | 0 or unbounded | 0 or unbounded | monotonic |
| [von Bertalanffy](#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy) | $a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | $x\ge c$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating |
| [Shepherd](#sec-fn-shepherd) | $\dfrac{ax}{b+x^c}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote if $c=1$, tends to 0 if $c>1$ | saturating, or one maximum if $c>1$ |
| [Hassell](#sec-fn-hassell) | $\dfrac{ax}{(b+x)^c}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote if $c=1$, tends to 0 if $c>1$ | saturating, or one maximum if $c>1$ |
| [Generalised Ricker](#sec-fn-generalised-ricker) | $a\left[\dfrac{x}{b}\,e^{1-x/b}\right]^c$ | $x\ge0$ | 0 | tends to 0 | one maximum of adjustable width |
| [Non-rectangular hyperbola](#sec-fn-nonrectangular) | $\dfrac{\alpha x+p_{\max}-\sqrt{(\alpha x+p_{\max})^2-4\theta\alpha x\,p_{\max}}}{2\theta}$ | $x\ge0$ | 0, straight line | asymptote | saturating, with a bend of adjustable sharpness |
| [Richards](#sec-fn-richards) | $\dfrac{a}{\left[1+d\,e^{-b(x-c)}\right]^{1/d}}$ | all $x$ | close to 0 | asymptote | sigmoid of adjustable asymmetry |

Several functions have the same properties in this table (e.g., the Michaelis–Menten and
the saturating exponential functions). The entries say how such functions differ and
which mechanism, if any, leads to each of them.

# Polynomials

A polynomial is a sum of powers of $x$, each multiplied by a parameter. The two
polynomials that are used most are the straight line and the parabola.

## Linear {#sec-fn-linear}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a + b * x} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{straight line} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \text{all } y \quad (b \neq 0) \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows or decreases without bound, slope } b \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{crosses zero at } x = -a/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad d + b(x - c),\ \text{with } d = a + bc \text{ the value at } x = c
\end{aligned}
$$

The linear function describes a response that changes by the same amount for every unit of
the predictor. It is a mechanistic function when a quantity accumulates or is lost at a
constant rate, as the quantity is then a linear function of time. More often it is a
phenomenological description over a limited range of $x$, since any smooth function is
close to a straight line over a short enough interval. In this book
the linear function is mostly used inside another function: $e^{a+bx}$ for a positive
response and $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a+bx)$ for a probability (see
[Range and composition](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-composition)).

The function is

$$
f(x)=a+bx,
$$

where $a$ is the value of the function at $x=0$ (the intercept) and $b$ is its slope. Both
parameters can be positive or negative. The
[derivative](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-derivatives) is the same at every $x$,

$$
f'(x)=b, \qquad f''(x)=0,
$$

so the function has neither curvature nor special points. It has no asymptote either: as
$x\to\infty$ it grows without bound when $b>0$ and decreases without bound when $b<0$. It
crosses zero at $x=-a/b$, so for a quantity that must be positive the function can only be
used on one side of that value.

The intercept $a$ depends on where the zero of $x$ lies, and it has no meaning when
$x=0$ is far from the values of interest (e.g., when $x$ is a calendar year). In that case
we write the function around a reference value $c$ that we choose,

$$
f(x)=d+b(x-c), \qquad d=a+bc,
$$

where $d$ is the value of the function at $x=c$. This is a
[reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation): the line is the
same, and the slope $b$ keeps its value and its meaning.

### Example: sediment in a pond

Suppose that the layer of sediment at the bottom of a pond was 12 cm thick when monitoring
started and that it grows by 0.4 cm per year. With $x$ the time in years since the start,
$a=12$ cm and $b=0.4$ cm per year. After 10 years the layer is

$$
f(10)=12+0.4\times10=16 \text{ cm}
$$

thick, and it reaches 20 cm when $12+0.4x=20$, that is, after $x=(20-12)/0.4=20$ years.
Written around year 10, the same line is $16+0.4(x-10)$. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Linear function: a is the value at x = 0 and b is the slope
linear = function(x, a = 0, b = 1) {
  a + b * x
}

# Thickness of the sediment after 10 years (cm)
linear(x = 10, a = 12, b = 0.4)

# Years until the layer is 20 cm thick
(20 - 12) / 0.4

# The same line written around year 10, at the start and after 25 years
16 + 0.4 * (c(0, 25) - 10)
linear(x = c(0, 25), a = 12, b = 0.4)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Linear functions with a = 12 and b = 0.4 (solid line) and with a = 20 and b = −0.5 (dashed line). The second line crosses zero at x = −a/b = 40."
x_values = seq(0, 50, length.out = 200)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(linear(x_values, a = 12, b = 0.4), linear(x_values, a = 20, b = -0.5)),
  curve = rep(c("a = 12, b = 0.4", "a = 20, b = -0.5"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: sprint speed of a lizard"}

The sprint speed of a lizard is 1.2 m per second at a body temperature of 20 °C and 2.0 m
per second at 30 °C. Find the parameters $a$ and $b$ of the straight line through these
two points, with their units. Which speed does the line give at 5 °C, and what does that
say about the range of temperatures over which it can be used?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The slope is the change in speed divided by the change in temperature,
$b=(2.0-1.2)/(30-20)=0.08$ m per second per °C. The intercept follows from one of the
points: $a=1.2-0.08\times20=-0.4$ m per second. At 5 °C the line gives
$-0.4+0.08\times5=0$ m per second, and below 5 °C it gives negative speeds. So $-a/b=5$ °C
is the lower end of the range over which this line can describe a speed, and the intercept
$a$ is the value of the line at 0 °C, a temperature at which it is of no use. Written
around 20 °C the line is $1.2+0.08(x-20)$.

:::
::::

## Quadratic {#sec-fn-quadratic}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a + b * x + c * x^2| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal when } c < 0;\ \text{U-shaped when } c > 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \leq a - b^2/(4c) \text{ when } c < 0;\quad y \geq a - b^2/(4c) \text{ when } c > 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope at } x = 0;\quad c = \text{half of the second derivative} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{decreases without bound when } c < 0,\ \text{grows without bound when } c > 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum or minimum at } x_{\max} = -b/(2c),\ \text{with value } a - b^2/(4c) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad f(x_{\max}) + c\,(x - x_{\max})^2
\end{aligned}
$$

The quadratic function, or parabola, is the simplest function with a maximum or a minimum.
It is used as a phenomenological description of a response that is highest at intermediate
values of the predictor (e.g., growth as a function of temperature), over a limited range
of $x$. It can also follow from geometry: a process that depends on a surface, such as the
area of the skin or of the mouth, is quadratic in the length of the organism. Finally,
every smooth function is close to a parabola near its maximum, which is the idea behind
the Wald interval of [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty).

Polynomials of a higher order (a cubic function has a term in $x^3$, and so on) add one
bend for every additional power and can follow almost any set of points. However, outside
the range of the data they grow or decrease without bound, in a direction that is decided
by the highest power alone, so their predictions there are unreliable.^[The extrapolation
of census counts with a polynomial is a well-known exercise on this problem; see Forsythe,
Malcolm and Moler (1977).] For that reason this supplement stops at the quadratic
function.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a+bx+cx^2,
$$

where $a$ is the value at $x=0$, $b$ is the slope at $x=0$ (in units of $y$ per unit of
$x$) and $c$ controls the curvature (in units of $y$ per unit of $x$ squared). The three
parameters can be positive or negative. The first two derivatives are

$$
f'(x)=b+2cx, \qquad f''(x)=2c.
$$

The second derivative has the same sign everywhere. When $c<0$ the function is concave for
every $x$ and its only [critical point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-maxima) is a
maximum; when $c>0$ it is convex and the critical point is a minimum. Setting $f'(x)=0$:

$$
x_{\max}=-\frac{b}{2c}, \qquad f(x_{\max})=a-\frac{b^2}{4c}.
$$

If we complete the square, we can write the function with these two landmarks as
parameters,

$$
f(x)=f(x_{\max})+c\,(x-x_{\max})^2,
$$

which shows that the parabola is symmetric around $x_{\max}$. It also shows that, when
$c<0$, the function crosses zero at $x_{\max}\pm\sqrt{f(x_{\max})/(-c)}$ and is negative
beyond those two values. A response that cannot be negative is therefore described by a
quadratic function only between them.

### Example: growth of a caterpillar and temperature

Suppose that the growth rate of a caterpillar (mg per day) as a function of temperature
$x$ (°C) is $f(x)=-6+1.2x-0.03x^2$. The units of the parameters are mg per day for $a$, mg
per day per °C for $b$ and mg per day per °C squared for $c$. The growth rate is highest
at

$$
x_{\max}=-\frac{1.2}{2\times(-0.03)}=20 \text{ °C},
\qquad
f(20)=-6+1.2\times20-0.03\times20^2=6 \text{ mg per day},
$$

so the function can be written as $6-0.03(x-20)^2$. It crosses zero at
$20\pm\sqrt{6/0.03}=20\pm14.1$, that is, at 5.9 and 34.1 °C, and it describes a growth rate
only between those temperatures. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Quadratic function: a is the value at x = 0, b the slope there, c the curvature
quadratic = function(x, a = 0, b = 0, c = 1) {
  a + b * x + c * x^2
}

# Location and value of the maximum from the formulas
-1.2 / (2 * -0.03)
-6 - 1.2^2 / (4 * -0.03)

# The same on a fine grid of temperatures
temperature_grid = seq(0, 40, by = 0.01)
growth_values = quadratic(temperature_grid, a = -6, b = 1.2, c = -0.03)
temperature_grid[which.max(growth_values)]
max(growth_values)

# Temperatures at which the function crosses zero (up to rounding error)
zero_growth = 20 + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(6 / 0.03)
zero_growth
quadratic(zero_growth, a = -6, b = 1.2, c = -0.03)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Quadratic functions with a maximum at x = 20 and a value of 6 there, for c = −0.03 (solid line; a = −6, b = 1.2) and c = −0.01 (dashed line; a = 2, b = 0.4). Dashed grey lines mark the maximum and the value zero."
x_values = seq(0, 40, length.out = 200)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(quadratic(x_values, a = -6, b = 1.2, c = -0.03),
        quadratic(x_values, a = 2, b = 0.4, c = -0.01)),
  curve = rep(c("c = -0.03", "c = -0.01"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("c = -0.03", "c = -0.01"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 6), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: species richness and productivity"}

The number of plant species in a grassland plot as a function of its productivity $x$ (t
per ha per year) is described by $f(x)=10+4x-0.25x^2$. At which productivity is the number
of species highest, and how many species does the function give there? Calculate the slope
at $x=0$ and at $x=12$, with units. At which productivity does the function return to its
value at $x=0$?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The maximum is at $x_{\max}=-4/(2\times(-0.25))=8$ t per ha per year, where the function
gives $10+32-16=26$ species. The derivative is $f'(x)=4-0.5x$, so the slope is 4 species
per t per ha per year at $x=0$ and $4-6=-2$ species per t per ha per year at $x=12$. The
parabola is symmetric around its maximum, so it returns to $f(0)=10$ species at twice the
location of the maximum, $x=16$ t per ha per year.

:::
::::

# Piecewise functions

A piecewise function is defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain.
The parts meet at a **breakpoint**, at which the function, its slope or both change
abruptly. In R these functions are written with `ifelse()` (see
[Functions in R](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-functions-r)).

## Threshold {#sec-fn-threshold}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a, b)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{step} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y = a \text{ or } y = b \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value below the threshold (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{value from the threshold onwards (units of } y\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{threshold (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At the left end}: &\quad f(x) = a,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) = b,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{jump of size } b - a \text{ at } x = c \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{the limit of } a + \dfrac{b - a}{1 + e^{-s(x - c)}} \text{ as } s \to \infty,\ \text{for } x \neq c
\end{aligned}
$$

The threshold function describes a response that switches between two levels when the
predictor crosses a critical value. It is used when an organism changes its behaviour or
its state abruptly, for example the number of eggs that a parasitoid lays on a host as a
function of the number of eggs that it carries (Hilborn and Mangel 1997; the original
study of Rosenheim and Rosen 1991 used a logistic function), and more generally for the
sharp transitions between strategies that models of optimal behaviour predict (Hilborn
and Mangel 1997). The function is mechanistic when theory predicts such a switch, and
otherwise it is the simplest phenomenological description of two levels.
[Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd) uses a threshold function to show what a jump does to
a likelihood.

The function is

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
a & \text{if } x<c \\
b & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the two levels, which can take any value, and $c$ is the threshold.
The formula has to say to which side the value $x=c$ belongs; here it belongs to the upper
piece. There is nothing to derive with calculus. The two limits are the two levels, and
the slope is zero everywhere except at $x=c$, where the function jumps by $b-a$ and has no
derivative. This has a consequence for estimation: moving $c$ by a small amount changes
the function only if an observation lies between the old and the new threshold, so the
methods that search for an optimum by following a slope fail for $c$ (Chapter 8).

A smooth function that approaches the threshold function is the
[logistic](#sec-fn-logistic) function with a lower level $a$,

$$
f(x)=a+\frac{b-a}{1+e^{-s(x-c)}},
$$

where $s$ is the steepness. The larger $s$ is, the shorter the range of $x$ over which the
function moves from $a$ to $b$, and as $s\to\infty$ it becomes the threshold function
everywhere except at the breakpoint: at $x=c$ the logistic function equals $(a+b)/2$ for
every $s$, whereas the threshold function equals $b$.

### Example: foraging of bumblebees and temperature

Suppose that the workers of a bumblebee colony stay in the nest below 10 °C and make 6
foraging trips per hour from that temperature onwards. With $x$ the air temperature,
$a=0$ trips per hour, $b=6$ trips per hour and $c=10$ °C. The function gives 0 trips per
hour at 8 °C and 6 trips per hour at 10 °C and at 14 °C. A logistic function with a
steepness $s=5$ per °C gives, half a degree below and half a degree above the threshold,

$$
\frac{6}{1+e^{-5\times(9.5-10)}}=\frac{6}{1+e^{2.5}}\approx0.46
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{6}{1+e^{-2.5}}\approx5.54
$$

trips per hour, so it completes most of the switch within one degree. We can verify our
math with R:

```{r}
# Threshold function: a below the threshold c and b from the threshold onwards
threshold = function(x, a = 0, b = 1, c = 1) {
  ifelse(x < c, a, b)
}

# Foraging trips per hour at 8, 10 and 14 degrees
threshold(x = c(8, 10, 14), a = 0, b = 6, c = 10)

# A logistic function with lower level a, upper level b and steepness s
smooth_threshold = function(x, a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, s = 1) {
  a + (b - a) / (1 + exp(-s * (x - c)))
}

# Half a degree below and above the threshold, for a steepness of 5 and of 50 per degree
smooth_threshold(x = c(9.5, 10.5), a = 0, b = 6, c = 10, s = 5)
smooth_threshold(x = c(9.5, 10.5), a = 0, b = 6, c = 10, s = 50)
```

With $s=50$ per °C the logistic function is indistinguishable from the threshold function
at these two temperatures.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Threshold function with a = 0, b = 6 and c = 10 (solid line) and logistic functions between the same two levels with a steepness s = 1 (dotted line) and s = 5 (dashed line). The dashed grey line marks the threshold."
x_values = seq(4, 16, length.out = 601)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(threshold(x_values, a = 0, b = 6, c = 10),
        smooth_threshold(x_values, a = 0, b = 6, c = 10, s = 5),
        smooth_threshold(x_values, a = 0, b = 6, c = 10, s = 1)),
  curve = rep(c("Threshold", "Logistic, s = 5", "Logistic, s = 1"),
              each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve,
                          levels = c("Threshold", "Logistic, s = 5", "Logistic, s = 1"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: seedling survival and soil water"}

The probability that a seedling survives the summer is 0.2 when the water content of the
soil is below 15% and 0.9 otherwise. Write this function as a formula and as a call to
`ifelse()`. What is the average survival probability over four plots with a water content
of 10, 14, 15 and 22%? What is the slope of the function at 20%?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The function is $f(x)=0.2$ if $x<15$ and $f(x)=0.9$ if $x\ge15$, that is,
`ifelse(x < 15, 0.2, 0.9)`. The four plots have survival probabilities of 0.2, 0.2, 0.9
and 0.9 (the plot at exactly 15% belongs to the upper piece), so the average is
$(0.2+0.2+0.9+0.9)/4=0.55$. The slope at 20% is zero: away from the threshold a change in
water content has no effect on survival.

:::
::::

## Hockey stick {#sec-fn-hockey-stick}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a * x, a * c)} \quad \text{or} \quad \texttt{pmin(a * x, a * c)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating, with a sharp corner} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \quad (x \geq 0 \text{ in most uses}) \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \leq ac \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{slope below the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
c = \text{breakpoint (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) = ac,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{breakpoint at } x = c,\ \text{where the slope changes from } a \text{ to } 0 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \min(ax, d),\ \text{with } d = ac \text{ the plateau}
\end{aligned}
$$

The hockey stick function describes a response that increases in proportion to the
predictor until it hits a ceiling. It has a mechanistic reading when a process runs at a
constant rate per unit of $x$ until a capacity is reached, as for filter feeders that
take up food in proportion to its concentration until they reach a maximum uptake (the
Holling type I functional response). It is also used for the number of recruits as a
function of the size of the spawning stock in fisheries (Barrowman and Myers 2000), for
the density dependence of populations of lemmings, sheep and moose (Framstad et al. 1997;
Grenfell et al. 1998; Post et al. 2002; Brännström and Sumpter 2005) and to locate the
edges between habitats in a landscape (Toms and Lesperance 2003). Bacon and Watts (1971,
1974) studied how to estimate the transition between two straight lines from data.

The function is

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
ax & \text{if } x<c \\
ac & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $a$ is the slope of the first piece and $c$ is the breakpoint. The two pieces meet
at $x=c$, where both give $ac$, so the function has no jump. Its slope does: the
derivative is $a$ for $x<c$ and 0 for $x>c$, and it does not exist at the breakpoint. The
plateau $ac$ can be used as a parameter in the place of the breakpoint, which gives
$\min(ax,d)$ with $d=ac$: the smaller of the straight line and the plateau, `pmin()` in R.

It is instructive to compare the hockey stick with the
[Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function that has the same initial slope $a$
and the same upper limit $ac$, which is $acx/(c+x)$. At $x=c$ the hockey stick has reached
its plateau, whereas the Michaelis–Menten function is at half of it: the breakpoint of
the one is the half-maximum of the other. The two functions are the extremes of a family
with a bend of adjustable sharpness, the
[non-rectangular hyperbola](#sec-fn-nonrectangular).

### Example: uptake of algae by a mussel

Suppose that a mussel clears the algae from 1.5 litres of water per hour, up to a
concentration of 40 µg of carbon per litre, beyond which its uptake stays constant. With
$x$ the concentration of algae (µg of carbon per litre) and $f(x)$ the uptake (µg of
carbon per hour), $a=1.5$ litres per hour and $c=40$ µg per litre. The plateau is
$ac=1.5\times40=60$ µg per hour. The uptake is

$$
f(10)=1.5\times10=15, \qquad f(40)=60, \qquad f(100)=60
$$

µg of carbon per hour. The Michaelis–Menten function with the same initial slope and upper
limit, $60x/(40+x)$, gives 12, 30 and 42.9 µg per hour at those concentrations. We can
verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Hockey stick function: slope a up to the breakpoint c, then the plateau a * c
hockey_stick = function(x, a = 1, c = 1) {
  ifelse(x < c, a * x, a * c)
}

# Uptake at 10, 40 and 100 micrograms of carbon per litre
concentrations = c(10, 40, 100)
hockey_stick(x = concentrations, a = 1.5, c = 40)

# The same with pmin(): the smaller of the line and the plateau
pmin(1.5 * concentrations, 60)

# Michaelis–Menten function with the same initial slope and upper limit
60 * concentrations / (40 + concentrations)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Hockey stick function with a = 1.5 and c = 40 (solid line) and the Michaelis–Menten function with the same initial slope and upper limit (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the breakpoint and the plateau ac = 60."
x_values = seq(0, 200, length.out = 401)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(hockey_stick(x_values, a = 1.5, c = 40), 60 * x_values / (40 + x_values)),
  curve = rep(c("Hockey stick", "Michaelis–Menten"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 60, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 40, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: recruits and spawners"}

The number of recruits of a fish stock increases by 3 recruits per spawner and levels off
at 600 recruits. Where is the breakpoint of this hockey stick function? How many recruits
does it give for 150 and for 450 spawners? Write the function with `pmin()`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The plateau is $ac=600$ recruits and the slope is $a=3$ recruits per spawner, so the
breakpoint is at $c=600/3=200$ spawners. For 150 spawners, below the breakpoint, the
function gives $3\times150=450$ recruits, and for 450 spawners it gives the plateau of 600
recruits. In R the function is `pmin(3 * x, 600)`.

:::
::::

## Piecewise linear {#sec-fn-piecewise-linear}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{ifelse(x < c, a + b * x, a + b * c + d * (x - c))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{two straight lines that meet at a corner} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad \text{all } y \text{ when } b \text{ and } d \text{ have the same sign};\quad
y \leq a + bc \text{ when } b > 0 > d \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{slope below the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{breakpoint (units of } x\text{)};\quad
d = \text{slope above the breakpoint (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } b \quad (c > 0) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows or decreases without bound, slope } d \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{breakpoint at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a + bc,\ \text{where the slope changes from } b \text{ to } d \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a + bx + (d - b)\max(0,\, x - c)
\end{aligned}
$$

The piecewise linear function describes a response that changes at one constant rate up to
a breakpoint and at another constant rate beyond it. It is the general form of the
functions of this group that have no jump: the [hockey stick](#sec-fn-hockey-stick) is the
case in which the first line starts at zero and the second one is flat. The function is
used when an organism is expected to switch from one regime to another at some value of
the predictor, for example from growing to reproducing once it has reached a certain size
or age, and to locate ecological thresholds in data (Toms and Lesperance 2003). It is
mechanistic when theory predicts the switch, and otherwise a phenomenological description
of a relationship that bends once.

The function is

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
a+bx & \text{if } x<c \\
a+bc+d\,(x-c) & \text{if } x\ge c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $a$ is the value at $x=0$, $b$ is the slope below the breakpoint $c$ and $d$ is the
slope above it. The parameters $a$, $b$ and $d$ can be positive or negative. The second
piece starts at $a+bc$, which is the value that the first piece reaches at $x=c$, so the
two lines meet and the function has no jump. Its derivative is $b$ for $x<c$ and $d$ for
$x>c$, and it does not exist at the breakpoint. When $b$ and $d$ have opposite signs the
breakpoint is the maximum ($b>0>d$) or the minimum ($b<0<d$) of the function, and it is
one that we cannot find by setting a derivative to zero.

The function can be written on a single line. The second piece is the first line plus a
correction of the slope that applies only beyond the breakpoint,

$$
f(x)=a+bx+(d-b)\max(0,\,x-c),
$$

where $\max(0,x-c)$ is zero up to the breakpoint and equal to the distance from it
afterwards (`pmax(0, x - c)` in R). In this form $d-b$ is the change in slope at the
breakpoint, and a function with several breakpoints is obtained by adding one such term
for each of them.

A piecewise linear function with many breakpoints can follow any relationship, at the cost
of a corner at each breakpoint. **Splines** remove the corners: they are piecewise cubic
functions whose pieces join smoothly at points called knots. They are used when we want a
smooth curve through the data and do not need to interpret its parameters (Wood 2001,
2006), so they are not described further in this supplement.

### Example: growth of a fish before and after maturity

Suppose that a fish is 4 cm long when it hatches, grows by 8 cm per year until it matures
at an age of 3 years, and by 2 cm per year afterwards, when part of its energy goes to
reproduction. With $x$ the age in years and $f(x)$ the length in cm, $a=4$ cm, $b=8$ cm
per year, $c=3$ years and $d=2$ cm per year. The length at maturity is
$a+bc=4+8\times3=28$ cm, and

$$
f(2)=4+8\times2=20 \text{ cm}, \qquad f(6)=28+2\times(6-3)=34 \text{ cm}.
$$

The fish reaches 40 cm when $28+2(x-3)=40$, that is, at an age of $x=3+12/2=9$ years. The
change in slope at maturity is $d-b=-6$ cm per year. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Piecewise linear function: value a at x = 0, slope b up to the breakpoint c
# and slope d from the breakpoint onwards
piecewise_linear = function(x, a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, d = 0) {
  ifelse(x < c, a + b * x, a + b * c + d * (x - c))
}

# Length (cm) at 2, 3 and 6 years
ages = c(2, 3, 6)
piecewise_linear(x = ages, a = 4, b = 8, c = 3, d = 2)

# The same on a single line, with pmax()
4 + 8 * ages + (2 - 8) * pmax(0, ages - 3)

# Age at which the fish is 40 cm long, and its length at that age
3 + (40 - 28) / 2
piecewise_linear(x = 9, a = 4, b = 8, c = 3, d = 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Piecewise linear functions with a = 4, b = 8 and c = 3, for a slope above the breakpoint d = 2 (solid line) and d = −2 (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the breakpoint and the value a + bc = 28 that both functions have there; with d < 0 the breakpoint is the maximum."
x_values = seq(0, 10, length.out = 401)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(piecewise_linear(x_values, a = 4, b = 8, c = 3, d = 2),
        piecewise_linear(x_values, a = 4, b = 8, c = 3, d = -2)),
  curve = rep(c("d = 2", "d = -2"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("d = 2", "d = -2"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 28, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: bird species and forest cover"}

The number of bird species in a landscape is 5 without forest and increases by 0.2 species
for every percent of forest cover up to a cover of 30%, and by 0.05 species per percent
beyond that. How many species does this piecewise linear function give at a cover of 30%
and of 100%? At which cover does it give 13 species? Write the function on a single line
with `pmax()`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The parameters are $a=5$ species, $b=0.2$ species per percent, $c=30$% and $d=0.05$
species per percent. At the breakpoint the function gives $a+bc=5+0.2\times30=11$ species,
and at a cover of 100% it gives $11+0.05\times(100-30)=14.5$ species. Since 13 species is
more than the value at the breakpoint, we solve $11+0.05(x-30)=13$, which gives
$x=30+2/0.05=70$%. The change in slope is $d-b=-0.15$ species per percent, so in R the
function is `5 + 0.2 * x - 0.15 * pmax(0, x - 30)`.

:::
::::

# Rational functions

A rational function is a ratio of two polynomials. Its limit as $x\to\infty$ is found by
dividing the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ (see
[Limits and asymptotes](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-limits)). Rational functions
approach their limits slowly, in proportion to a power of $x$.

## Hyperbolic {#sec-fn-hyperbolic}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a / (b + x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{decreasing, convex} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a/b \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{numerator (units of } y \text{ times units of } x\text{)};\quad
b = \text{value of } x \text{ at which the function has halved (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/b,\ \text{slope } -a/b^2 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half of the initial value at } x = b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{y_0}{1 + x/b},\ \text{with } y_0 = a/b \text{ the value at } x = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The hyperbolic function describes a response that declines towards zero, fast at first and
then more and more slowly. It is used for the performance of an individual as a function
of the density of its neighbours, for example the number of seeds that a plant produces as
a function of the number of plants around it (Pacala and Silander 1987, 1990). The
constant $b$ in the denominator keeps the function finite at $x=0$, where the simpler form
$a/x$ would be infinite. A mechanistic derivation exists when a total saturates: if the
total seed production of a stand follows the Michaelis–Menten function $ax/(b+x)$ of its
density $x$, the production per plant is that total divided by $x$, which is $a/(b+x)$.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{b+x},
$$

where $b$ has the units of $x$ and $a$ has the units of $y$ multiplied by those of $x$.
At $x=0$ the function equals $a/b$, and as $x\to\infty$ the denominator grows without
bound, so $f(x)\to0$. For large $x$ the function is close to $a/x$. Writing it as
$a(b+x)^{-1}$, the power rule and the chain rule give

$$
f'(x)=-\frac{a}{(b+x)^2}, \qquad f''(x)=\frac{2a}{(b+x)^3}.
$$

The slope is negative and the second derivative positive for every $x\ge0$, so the
function decreases and is convex everywhere. Its steepest slope is the one at zero,
$-a/b^2$. The parameter $b$ is a scale parameter (see
[Half-maxima and characteristic scales](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-scales)): if
we solve $a/(b+x)=a/(2b)$ for $x$ we find $x=b$, so $b$ is the value of $x$ at which the
function has fallen to half of its initial value. In the same way it has fallen to a third
at $x=2b$ and to a quarter at $x=3b$. Since the value at zero is easier to read from a
plot than $a$, the function is also written as $y_0/(1+x/b)$ with $y_0=a/b$.

### Example: plant biomass and density

Suppose that the mean biomass of a plant (g per plant) in a pot with $x$ plants is
$f(x)=60/(5+x)$, so that $b=5$ plants per pot and $a=60$ g per pot. A plant without
neighbours would weigh $f(0)=60/5=12$ g. The biomass per plant is

$$
f(5)=\frac{60}{5+5}=6 \text{ g}, \qquad f(15)=\frac{60}{5+15}=3 \text{ g},
$$

half and a quarter of that value. The slope at zero is $-60/5^2=-2.4$ g per plant for
every additional plant in the pot. The total biomass in the pot is $x\,f(x)=60x/(5+x)$, a
Michaelis–Menten function that approaches $a=60$ g per pot, which gives $a$ its meaning
here: it is the highest biomass that a pot can hold. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Hyperbolic function: starts at a / b and has halved at x = b
hyperbolic = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a / (b + x)
}

# Biomass per plant (g) without neighbours, at 5 and at 15 plants per pot
hyperbolic(x = c(0, 5, 15), a = 60, b = 5)

# Slope at zero: D() and the formula derived on paper
hyperbolic_derivative = D(expression(a / (b + x)), "x")
eval(hyperbolic_derivative, list(a = 60, b = 5, x = 0))
-60 / 5^2

# Total biomass per pot (g) at 5, 15 and 1000 plants per pot
c(5, 15, 1000) * hyperbolic(x = c(5, 15, 1000), a = 60, b = 5)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Hyperbolic functions that start at a/b = 12, with b = 5 (solid line; a = 60) and b = 15 (dashed line; a = 180). Dashed grey lines mark half of the initial value, which each function reaches at x = b."
x_values = seq(0, 60, length.out = 300)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(hyperbolic(x_values, a = 60, b = 5), hyperbolic(x_values, a = 180, b = 15)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 5", "b = 15"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("b = 5", "b = 15"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 15), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: seed production and neighbours"}

An isolated plant of an annual weed produces 200 seeds, and a plant with 8 neighbours per
m² produces half of that. Find the parameters $a$ and $b$ of a hyperbolic function with
these properties, with their units. At which density of neighbours does a plant produce
50 seeds?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The function has halved at $x=b$, so $b=8$ plants per m². The value at zero is $a/b=200$
seeds, so $a=200\times8=1600$ seeds times plants per m². For 50 seeds we solve
$1600/(8+x)=50$, which gives $8+x=32$ and $x=24$ plants per m². That is $3b$, the density
at which the function has fallen to a quarter of its initial value.

:::
::::

## Michaelis–Menten {#sec-fn-michaelis-menten}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * x / (b + x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{half-maximum (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{\alpha x}{1 + \alpha Hx},\ \text{with } a = 1/H \text{ and } b = 1/(\alpha H)
\end{aligned}
$$

The Michaelis–Menten function describes a response that increases in proportion to the
predictor when the predictor is scarce and levels off when it is abundant, because
something else then limits the response. It is one of the two functions of
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd), where its properties are derived step by step, and
it has a different name in almost every field that uses it. In biochemistry it is the rate
of a reaction catalysed by an enzyme as a function of the concentration of the substrate
(Michaelis and Menten 1913), with the parameters written as $v_{\max}$ and $K_m$. In
microbiology it is the Monod equation for the growth rate of micro-organisms on a limiting
nutrient (Monod 1949). In fisheries it is the Beverton–Holt curve for the number of
recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock (Beverton and Holt 1957). In
ecology it is best known as the Holling type II functional response, the feeding rate of a
predator as a function of the density of its prey (Holling 1959).

The function is mechanistic in each of these uses.
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-mechanistic) derives it for a predator that
divides its time between searching for prey and handling them, and the Beverton–Holt curve
follows from a mortality rate of the young fish that increases linearly with their density
(Quinn and Deriso 1999). The function is also used phenomenologically for any response
that rises from zero and saturates.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x},
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, with the units of $y$, and $b$ is the half-maximum, with the
units of $x$. Chapter 5 shows that $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)\to a$ as $x\to\infty$, and that

$$
f'(x)=\frac{ab}{(b+x)^2}, \qquad f''(x)=-\frac{2ab}{(b+x)^3},
$$

so the function increases and is concave for every $x\ge0$, with an initial slope of
$a/b$. To find the value of $x$ at which the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its
asymptote we solve $f(x_p)=pa$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a\,x_p}{b+x_p} &= pa \\
x_p &= p\,(b+x_p) \\
x_p &= \frac{p}{1-p}\,b .
\end{aligned}
$$

For $p=1/2$ this gives the half-maximum, $x_{1/2}=b$. For $p=0.9$ it gives $9b$ and for
$p=0.95$ it gives $19b$: the function approaches its asymptote slowly, and data that stop
at a few times the half-maximum are still far below it.

The parameterisations in use differ in which two landmarks they take as parameters (see
[Reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation)):

| Parameters | Formula | Conversion |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Asymptote $a$ and half-maximum $b$ | $\dfrac{ax}{b+x}$ | |
| Attack rate $\alpha$ and handling time $H$ (Holling type II) | $\dfrac{\alpha x}{1+\alpha Hx}$ | $a=1/H$, $b=1/(\alpha H)$ |
| Asymptote $a$ and initial slope $s$ | $\dfrac{asx}{a+sx}$ | $s=a/b$ |

The attack rate $\alpha$ of the second form is the initial slope $s$ of the third one.

### Example: growth of algae and phosphate

Suppose that the growth rate of a population of algae (per day) as a function of the
concentration of phosphate $x$ (µmol per litre) is $f(x)=1.2x/(0.5+x)$. The asymptote is
$a=1.2$ per day and the half-maximum is $b=0.5$ µmol per litre. The growth rate is

$$
f(0.5)=\frac{1.2\times0.5}{0.5+0.5}=0.6 \text{ per day},
\qquad
f(2)=\frac{1.2\times2}{0.5+2}=0.96 \text{ per day},
$$

half and 80% of the asymptote (note that $2=4b$, which is $p/(1-p)$ times $b$ for
$p=0.8$). The initial slope is $a/b=2.4$ per day per µmol per litre, and the algae need
$19b=9.5$ µmol per litre to grow at 95% of their maximum rate. We can verify our math with
R:

```{r}
# Michaelis–Menten function: asymptote a and half-maximum b
michaelis_menten = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x)
}

# Growth rate (per day) at 0.5 and 2 micromol per litre
michaelis_menten(x = c(0.5, 2), a = 1.2, b = 0.5)

# Concentrations at which the function reaches 80%, 90% and 95% of its asymptote
fractions = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95)
fractions / (1 - fractions) * 0.5
michaelis_menten(x = c(2, 4.5, 9.5), a = 1.2, b = 0.5) / 1.2

# The same function written with the attack rate and the handling time,
# and with the asymptote and the initial slope
alpha = 1.2 / 0.5
H = 1 / 1.2
alpha * c(0.5, 2) / (1 + alpha * H * c(0.5, 2))
1.2 * 2.4 * c(0.5, 2) / (1.2 + 2.4 * c(0.5, 2))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Michaelis–Menten functions with an asymptote a = 1.2 (dashed grey line) and a half-maximum b = 0.5 (solid line) and b = 2 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the two half-maxima, at which each function reaches a/2 = 0.6."
x_values = seq(0, 10, length.out = 300)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(michaelis_menten(x_values, a = 1.2, b = 0.5),
        michaelis_menten(x_values, a = 1.2, b = 2)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.5", "b = 2"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.6, 1.2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: nectar intake of a bumblebee"}

The nectar intake of a bumblebee (µl per minute) increases with the density of flowers and
approaches 50 µl per minute. At a density of 12 flowers per m² the intake is 40 µl per
minute. Find the half-maximum $b$ of a Michaelis–Menten function with these properties.
What is its initial slope, and which density of flowers gives 90% of the maximum intake?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

An intake of 40 µl per minute is a fraction $p=0.8$ of the asymptote $a=50$ µl per minute,
and that fraction is reached at $x_p=\dfrac{p}{1-p}\,b=4b$. So $4b=12$ and $b=3$ flowers
per m². The initial slope is $a/b=50/3\approx16.7$ µl per minute per flower per m², and
90% of the maximum intake requires $9b=27$ flowers per m².

:::
::::

## Holling type III {#sec-fn-holling3}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{half-maximum (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = b;\ \text{inflection point at } x = b/\sqrt{3},\ \text{with value } a/4 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{\alpha x^2}{1 + \alpha Hx^2},\ \text{with } a = 1/H \text{ and } b = 1/\sqrt{\alpha H}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Holling type III function describes a response that increases slowly when the
predictor is scarce, accelerates and then levels off. It is the
[Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function with $x$ replaced by $x^2$ and the
half-maximum by its square, which turns a saturating function into a sigmoid one. As a
functional response it describes predators that kill a smaller proportion of the prey when
the prey are rare, which can result from predators that switch from rare to common prey,
from predators that aggregate where prey are abundant and from other forms of
heterogeneity (Morris 1997). A mechanistic derivation exists: if the attack rate of the
[disc equation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-mechanistic) is proportional to the density
of the prey, $\alpha x$ in the place of $\alpha$, the equation becomes
$\alpha x^2/(1+\alpha Hx^2)$.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax^2}{b^2+x^2},
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, with the units of $y$, and $b$ is the half-maximum, with the
units of $x$. At $x=0$ the function is zero. For small $x$ the denominator is close to
$b^2$, so $f(x)\approx(a/b^2)\,x^2$: the function starts as a parabola, with a slope of
zero. Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $x^2$ gives $a/(b^2/x^2+1)$, which
tends to $a$ as $x\to\infty$. The quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{2ax\left(b^2+x^2\right)-ax^2\times2x}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^2}
=\frac{2ab^2x}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^2}, \\
f''(x) &= \frac{2ab^2\left(b^2-3x^2\right)}{\left(b^2+x^2\right)^3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The slope is positive for every $x>0$, so the function increases. The second derivative is
zero where $b^2-3x^2=0$, positive below that value and negative above it, so the
[inflection point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-inflection) is at

$$
x=\frac{b}{\sqrt{3}}\approx0.58\,b, \qquad
f\left(\frac{b}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{a\,b^2/3}{b^2+b^2/3}=\frac{a}{4},
$$

where the slope has its largest value, $3\sqrt{3}\,a/(8b)\approx0.65\,a/b$. Unlike the
logistic function, the Holling type III function is asymmetric: it is steepest at a
quarter of its asymptote.

To find where the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its asymptote we solve
$x_p^2=p\left(b^2+x_p^2\right)$, which gives

$$
x_p=b\sqrt{\frac{p}{1-p}}.
$$

For $p=1/2$ this is the half-maximum, $x_{1/2}=b$, and for $p=0.9$ it is $3b$, against
$9b$ for the Michaelis–Menten function: the square makes the function approach its
asymptote faster. In the form with the attack rate, $H$ is the handling time and $\alpha$
has the units of $y$ per unit of $x$ squared, with $a=1/H$ and $b=1/\sqrt{\alpha H}$.

### Example: a bird that feeds on caterpillars

Suppose that the number of caterpillars that a bird eats per hour, as a function of the
density of caterpillars $x$ (caterpillars per m²), is $f(x)=40x^2/(36+x^2)$. The asymptote
is $a=40$ caterpillars per hour and the half-maximum is $b=6$ caterpillars per m². At a
density of 2, 6 and 18 caterpillars per m² the bird eats

$$
f(2)=\frac{40\times4}{36+4}=4, \qquad f(6)=\frac{40\times36}{36+36}=20, \qquad
f(18)=\frac{40\times324}{36+324}=36
$$

caterpillars per hour, that is, 10%, 50% and 90% of the asymptote. A Michaelis–Menten
function with the same parameters gives $40\times2/(6+2)=10$ caterpillars per hour at the
lowest of these densities, more than twice as many. The intake increases fastest at
$6/\sqrt{3}\approx3.5$ caterpillars per m², where it is $a/4=10$ caterpillars per hour and
increases by $3\sqrt{3}\times40/(8\times6)\approx4.3$ caterpillars per hour for every
additional caterpillar per m². We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Holling type III function: asymptote a and half-maximum b
holling_3 = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)
}

# Caterpillars eaten per hour at 2, 6 and 18 caterpillars per square metre
holling_3(x = c(2, 6, 18), a = 40, b = 6)

# Michaelis–Menten function with the same parameters at the lowest density
40 * 2 / (6 + 2)

# Inflection point: location, value, and slope from D() and from the formula
x_inflection = 6 / sqrt(3)
x_inflection
holling_3(x = x_inflection, a = 40, b = 6)
holling_3_derivative = D(expression(a * x^2 / (b^2 + x^2)), "x")
eval(holling_3_derivative, list(a = 40, b = 6, x = x_inflection))
3 * sqrt(3) * 40 / (8 * 6)

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection point
eval(D(holling_3_derivative, "x"), list(a = 40, b = 6, x = x_inflection))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Holling type III function with an asymptote a = 40 and a half-maximum b = 6 (solid line) and the Michaelis–Menten function with the same parameters (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the asymptote, half of it and the half-maximum, which the two functions share."
x_values = seq(0, 40, length.out = 400)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(holling_3(x_values, a = 40, b = 6), 40 * x_values / (6 + x_values)),
  curve = rep(c("Holling type III", "Michaelis–Menten"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(20, 40), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 6, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: a kestrel that hunts voles"}

The number of voles that a kestrel kills per week approaches 12 at high densities of
voles, and it is 6 voles per week at a density of 20 voles per ha. Find the parameters of
a Holling type III function with these properties, with their units. At which density
does the kill rate increase fastest, and what is the kill rate there? Which density gives
80% of the maximum kill rate?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The asymptote is $a=12$ voles per week, and half of it is reached at the half-maximum, so
$b=20$ voles per ha. The kill rate increases fastest at the inflection point,
$b/\sqrt{3}=20/1.732\approx11.5$ voles per ha, where it is $a/4=3$ voles per week. A
fraction $p=0.8$ of the asymptote is reached at $b\sqrt{p/(1-p)}=20\sqrt{4}=40$ voles per
ha.

:::
::::

## Holling type IV {#sec-fn-holling4}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid when } c \geq 0;\ \text{unimodal, with an asymptote, when } c < 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y \leq 4ab/(4b - c^2) \text{ when } c < 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b > 0 \text{ (units of } x \text{ squared)};\quad c \text{ (units of } x\text{), with } c^2 < 4b \text{ when } c < 0 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{from below when } c \geq 0 \text{ and from above when } c < 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c < 0,\ \text{maximum at } x = -2b/c \text{ with value } 4ab/(4b - c^2) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{with } c = 0,\ \text{the Holling type III function } ax^2/(b + x^2)
\end{aligned}
$$

The Holling type IV function adds a term in $x$ to the denominator of the
[Holling type III](#sec-fn-holling3) function, and the sign of its parameter $c$ decides
the shape. When $c>0$ the function is sigmoid, and it has a mechanistic derivation: it is
the functional response of a predator whose attack rate is itself a Michaelis–Menten
function of the density of the prey, that is, a predator that pursues prey more actively
when they are abundant (Turchin 2003). When $c<0$ the function rises above its asymptote,
reaches a maximum and declines towards the asymptote. In that form it is used
phenomenologically for the intake of a consumer that declines at high density, as a
result of interference among predators or of defences induced in the prey (Holt 1983;
Collings 1997; Wilmshurst et al. 1999; Chen 2004).

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax^2}{b+cx+x^2},
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, $b$ is positive and has the units of $x$ squared, and $c$ has
the units of $x$ and can be positive or negative. Note that $b$ is here the counterpart
of $b^2$ in the Holling type III function. The limits are found as for that function:
$f(0)=0$ with a slope of zero, since $f(x)\approx(a/b)\,x^2$ for small $x$, and
$f(x)\to a$ as $x\to\infty$, since dividing by $x^2$ gives $a/(b/x^2+c/x+1)$. The
denominator has to stay positive for every $x\ge0$. That is always so when $c\ge0$. When
$c<0$ the denominator is smallest at $x=-c/2$, where it equals $b-c^2/4$, so the function
requires $c^2<4b$.

The quotient rule gives a derivative whose numerator simplifies:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{2ax\left(b+cx+x^2\right)-ax^2\left(c+2x\right)}{\left(b+cx+x^2\right)^2} \\
&= \frac{ax\left(2b+cx\right)}{\left(b+cx+x^2\right)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

A quotient is zero only where its numerator is zero (see
[Maxima and minima](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-maxima)), so the critical points
are $x=0$ and the solution of $2b+cx=0$. When $c\ge0$ the factor $2b+cx$ is positive for
every $x\ge0$ and the function increases throughout. When $c<0$ the slope is positive up
to

$$
x_{\max}=-\frac{2b}{c}
$$

and negative beyond it, so this is a maximum. Its value follows from substituting
$x_{\max}$ in the function. The denominator is $b-2b+4b^2/c^2=b\left(4b-c^2\right)/c^2$
and the numerator is $4ab^2/c^2$, so

$$
f(x_{\max})=\frac{4ab}{4b-c^2},
$$

which is larger than $a$: the function overshoots its asymptote and returns to it from
above. The closer $c^2$ is to $4b$, the higher the peak.

### Example: intake of a grazer and biomass of grass

Suppose that the intake of a gazelle (g of grass per minute) as a function of the biomass
of grass $x$ (g per m²) is $f(x)=6x^2/(400-20x+x^2)$, so that $a=6$ g per minute, $b=400$
(g per m²)² and $c=-20$ g per m². The condition $c^2<4b$ holds, as $400<1600$. The intake
is highest at

$$
x_{\max}=-\frac{2\times400}{-20}=40 \text{ g per m}^2,
\qquad
f(40)=\frac{4\times6\times400}{4\times400-(-20)^2}=\frac{9600}{1200}=8 \text{ g per minute},
$$

and at a biomass of 200 g per m² it has fallen to
$6\times40000/(400-4000+40000)\approx6.6$ g per minute, on its way down to the asymptote
of 6 g per minute. With $c=20$ g per m² and the same $a$ and $b$, the function is sigmoid
and gives $6\times1600/(400+800+1600)\approx3.4$ g per minute at 40 g per m². We can
verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Holling type IV function: asymptote a and parameters b and c of the denominator
holling_4 = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a * x^2 / (b + c * x + x^2)
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of biomass
biomass_grid = seq(0, 400, by = 0.01)
intake_values = holling_4(biomass_grid, a = 6, b = 400, c = -20)
biomass_grid[which.max(intake_values)]
max(intake_values)

# The values derived on paper: -2 * b / c and 4 * a * b / (4 * b - c^2)
-2 * 400 / -20
4 * 6 * 400 / (4 * 400 - (-20)^2)

# Intake at 200 and at 10000 g per square metre
holling_4(x = c(200, 10000), a = 6, b = 400, c = -20)

# With a positive c the function is sigmoid: intake at 40 g per square metre
holling_4(x = 40, a = 6, b = 400, c = 20)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Holling type IV functions with a = 6 and b = 400, for c = −20 (solid line), c = 0 (dashed line; a Holling type III function with a half-maximum of 20) and c = 20 (dotted line). Dashed grey lines mark the asymptote and the location of the maximum of the solid curve, −2b/c = 40."
x_values = seq(0, 300, length.out = 600)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(holling_4(x_values, a = 6, b = 400, c = -20),
        holling_4(x_values, a = 6, b = 400, c = 0),
        holling_4(x_values, a = 6, b = 400, c = 20)),
  curve = rep(c("c = -20", "c = 0", "c = 20"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("c = -20", "c = 0", "c = 20"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 6, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 40, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: the condition on c"}

A Holling type IV function has $a=5$ and $b=9$. For $c=-3$, find the location and the
value of its maximum. Then explain what happens to the function when $c=-6$.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

For $c=-3$ the condition $c^2<4b$ holds ($9<36$). The maximum is at
$x_{\max}=-2b/c=-18/(-3)=6$, with value $4ab/(4b-c^2)=180/(36-9)\approx6.67$, a third
above the asymptote $a=5$. For $c=-6$ we have $c^2=4b=36$, and the denominator is
$9-6x+x^2=(x-3)^2$, which is zero at $x=3$. The function grows without bound as $x$
approaches 3, so it cannot describe a response there. This is why the function requires
$c^2<4b$ when $c$ is negative.

:::
::::

# Exponential functions

The functions of this group are built from the exponential function $e^{-bx}$, in which
the parameter $b$ is a rate with the inverse units of $x$. They approach their limits
faster than the rational functions of the same shape, because an exponential dominates any
power of $x$.

## Exponential {#sec-fn-exponential}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * exp(-b * x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{decreasing, convex (decay)};\quad \text{increasing, convex (growth, } ae^{bx}\text{)} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 0 \text{ (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a,\ \text{slope } -ab \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{halves every } \log 2/b;\ \text{falls by a factor } e \text{ every } 1/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\,e^{-x/c} \text{ with } c = 1/b;\quad e^{d - bx} \text{ with } d = \log a
\end{aligned}
$$

The exponential function describes a quantity that changes by a constant proportion for
every unit of the predictor. It is mechanistic whenever the rate of change of a quantity
is proportional to the quantity itself: a cohort in which every individual has the same
risk of dying per unit of time, litter that loses a constant fraction of its mass per day,
or light that loses a constant fraction of its intensity in every layer of leaves of a
canopy (Monsi and Saeki 1953). With a positive exponent, $ae^{bx}$, it describes the
growth of a population in which every individual reproduces at a constant rate.

The function is

$$
f(x)=ae^{-bx},
$$

where $a$ is the value at $x=0$, since $e^{0}=1$, and $b$ is the rate of decline. As
$x\to\infty$, $e^{-bx}=1/e^{bx}\to0$, so $f(x)\to0$. The rule for a constant multiple and
the rule for the exponential give $f'(x)=-ab\,e^{-bx}=-b\,f(x)$: the slope is negative for
every $x$, and at any point it is proportional to the value of the function. The second derivative,
$f''(x)=ab^2e^{-bx}$, is positive, so the function is convex.

The function has no special point, and what characterises it is a scale. An increase of
$x$ by one unit multiplies the function by $e^{-b}$, wherever we start, so a fraction
$1-e^{-b}$ is lost per unit of $x$. To find the distance over which the function falls to
a fraction $p$ of its value we solve $e^{-bx}=p$:

$$
x_p=\frac{\log(1/p)}{b}.
$$

For $p=1/2$ this is the half-life $\log 2/b\approx0.69/b$, for $p=1/e$ it is the
characteristic scale $1/b$, and for $p=0.05$ it is $\log(20)/b\approx3/b$. For exponential
growth the same algebra gives the doubling time, $\log 2/b$.

Taking logarithms gives $\log f(x)=\log a-bx$: on a plot with a logarithmic $y$ axis the
exponential function is a straight line with slope $-b$. In the other direction, the exponential of a straight line, $e^{d-bx}$, is an exponential
function with $a=e^{d}$. This is the form used when the function is the mean of a count,
since it is positive for any value of $d$ and $b$.

### Example: light in a canopy

Suppose that the light above a crop is 1500 µmol per m² per second and that it decreases
with the leaf area above the point of measurement, $x$ (m² of leaves per m² of ground,
counted from the top of the canopy), as $f(x)=1500e^{-0.6x}$. The parameter $a=1500$ µmol
per m² per second is the light above the canopy and $b=0.6$ per unit of leaf area is the
rate of decline. Below two and below four units of leaf area the light is

$$
f(2)=1500e^{-1.2}\approx452, \qquad f(4)=1500e^{-2.4}\approx136
$$

µmol per m² per second. Every unit of leaf area intercepts a fraction
$1-e^{-0.6}\approx0.45$ of the light that reaches it. The light is halved every
$\log 2/0.6\approx1.16$ units of leaf area, and the canopy intercepts 95% of the light
when $x=\log(20)/0.6\approx5.0$. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Exponential decay: value a at x = 0 and rate of decline b
exponential_decay = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * exp(-b * x)
}

# Light below 2 and 4 units of leaf area
exponential_decay(x = c(2, 4), a = 1500, b = 0.6)

# Fraction intercepted per unit of leaf area
1 - exp(-0.6)

# Leaf area over which the light is halved, and leaf area that intercepts 95%
log(2) / 0.6
log(20) / 0.6
exponential_decay(x = log(20) / 0.6, a = 1500, b = 0.6) / 1500
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Exponential functions. Left: exponential decay with a = 1500 for b = 0.6 (solid line) and b = 0.3 (dashed line); dashed grey lines mark half of the initial value and the two half-lives, log(2)/b. Right: exponential growth, a exp(bx), with a = 50 for b = 0.23 (solid line) and b = 0.12 (dashed line)."
library(patchwork)

x_values = seq(0, 8, length.out = 300)
decay_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(exponential_decay(x_values, a = 1500, b = 0.6),
        exponential_decay(x_values, a = 1500, b = 0.3)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.6", "b = 0.3"), each = length(x_values))
)
decay_data$curve = factor(decay_data$curve, levels = c("b = 0.6", "b = 0.3"))

x_growth = seq(0, 12, length.out = 300)
growth_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_growth, times = 2),
  y = c(50 * exp(0.23 * x_growth), 50 * exp(0.12 * x_growth)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.23", "b = 0.12"), each = length(x_growth))
)
growth_data$curve = factor(growth_data$curve, levels = c("b = 0.23", "b = 0.12"))

panel_decay = ggplot(decay_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 750, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(2) / c(0.6, 0.3), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Decay", x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()

panel_growth = ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Growth", x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()

panel_decay + panel_growth
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: duckweed on a pond"}

The number of duckweed fronds on a pond grows exponentially, $ae^{bx}$, where $x$ is the
time in days. There are 50 fronds at the start and their number doubles every 3 days. Find
$b$, with its units. By which factor does the number of fronds grow per day, and how many
fronds are there after 10 days?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The doubling time is $\log 2/b=3$ days, so $b=\log 2/3\approx0.231$ per day. Every day the
number of fronds is multiplied by $e^{b}=2^{1/3}\approx1.26$, an increase of 26% per day.
After 10 days there are $50e^{0.231\times10}=50\times2^{10/3}\approx504$ fronds, which is a
little more than three doublings ($50\times2^3=400$).

:::
::::

## Saturating exponential {#sec-fn-monomolecular}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * (1 - exp(-b * x))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } ab \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half-maximum at } x = \log 2/b;\ \text{a fraction } 1 - 1/e \text{ of the asymptote at } x = 1/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad d + a\left(1 - e^{-bx}\right),\ \text{which starts at } d \text{ and approaches } d + a
\end{aligned}
$$

The saturating exponential function describes a response that approaches an upper limit,
at a rate that is proportional to the distance that remains to that limit. This is its
mechanism, and it appears under several names. It is also called the
monomolecular function. In epidemiology it is the catalytic curve, the fraction of a cohort that has
been infected by a given age when the risk of infection per unit of time is constant
(Anderson and May 1991). It is the simplest form of the
[von Bertalanffy](#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy) growth curve (Essington et al. 2001), and it
was used by Skellam (1951) for the number of offspring as a function of the number of
adults (see also Brännström and Sumpter 2005). In this book it is the response function
of the practical of [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) and of
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd).

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right),
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote and $b$ is the rate at which the function approaches it. At
$x=0$ the exponential equals 1 and $f(0)=0$; as $x\to\infty$ the exponential tends to
zero and $f(x)\to a$. The derivatives are

$$
f'(x)=ab\,e^{-bx}, \qquad f''(x)=-ab^2e^{-bx},
$$

so the function increases, with an initial slope $ab$, and is concave everywhere. Note
that $f'(x)=b\left(a-f(x)\right)$: the slope is proportional to the distance to the
asymptote. To find where the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its asymptote we solve
$1-e^{-bx}=p$:

$$
x_p=\frac{\log\left(1/(1-p)\right)}{b}.
$$

The half-maximum is $x_{1/2}=\log 2/b$. At the characteristic scale $x=1/b$ the function
has reached $1-1/e\approx63\%$ of its asymptote, and it reaches 90% at
$\log(10)/b\approx2.3/b$. A [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function with the
same asymptote and the same initial slope has its half-maximum at $1/b$ and reaches 90%
only at $9/b$, so the saturating exponential bends more sharply towards its asymptote.

Two shifted and scaled forms of this function are used in later chapters (see
[Shifting and scaling](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts)). The first one adds
a value at zero,

$$
f(x)=d+a\left(1-e^{-bx}\right),
$$

which starts at $d$ and approaches $d+a$; Chapters 6 and 7 write it as
$r+a\left(1-e^{-kx}\right)$ for the response of photosynthesis to light. The second one
takes the value at zero, $y_0$, and the asymptote, $y_\infty$, as parameters,

$$
f(x)=y_\infty-\left(y_\infty-y_0\right)e^{-bx},
$$

and it is the same function with $d=y_0$ and $a=y_\infty-y_0$; the practical of Chapter 7
writes it as $A-(A-R_0)e^{-kt}$ for the growth of trees.

### Example: infection and age

Suppose that the animals of a population are exposed to a parasite at a constant rate of
0.4 infections per animal per year from birth, and that an infected animal remains
recognisable as such. The fraction of animals of age $x$ (years) that has been infected is
then $f(x)=1-e^{-0.4x}$, a saturating exponential with $a=1$ (a fraction, without units)
and $b=0.4$ per year. At an age of 1 and of 5 years:

$$
f(1)=1-e^{-0.4}\approx0.33, \qquad f(5)=1-e^{-2}\approx0.86.
$$

Half of the animals have been infected at an age of $\log 2/0.4\approx1.7$ years and 90%
at $\log(10)/0.4\approx5.8$ years. The initial slope is $ab=0.4$ per year, the rate of
infection itself.

For the shifted form, suppose that the net photosynthesis of a leaf (µmol per m² per
second) as a function of light $x$ (µmol per m² per second) is
$f(x)=-1.5+16.5\left(1-e^{-0.004x}\right)$. It starts at $d=-1.5$ in the dark and
approaches $d+a=15$. At $x=500$ it is $-1.5+16.5\left(1-e^{-2}\right)\approx12.8$, and it
is zero at the light intensity that solves $16.5\left(1-e^{-0.004x}\right)=1.5$, that is,
at $x=\log\left(1/(1-1.5/16.5)\right)/0.004\approx23.8$ µmol per m² per second. We can
verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Saturating exponential: asymptote a and rate b
saturating_exponential = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * (1 - exp(-b * x))
}

# Fraction infected at 1 and 5 years
saturating_exponential(x = c(1, 5), a = 1, b = 0.4)

# Ages at which 50% and 90% of the animals have been infected
log(2) / 0.4
log(10) / 0.4

# Shifted form for photosynthesis: value in the dark, at x = 500 and where it is
# zero (up to rounding error)
light_values = c(0, 500, log(1 / (1 - 1.5 / 16.5)) / 0.004)
light_values
-1.5 + saturating_exponential(x = light_values, a = 16.5, b = 0.004)

# The same function written with the value at zero and the asymptote
15 - (15 - -1.5) * exp(-0.004 * light_values)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Saturating exponential functions with an asymptote a = 1 (dashed grey line) and a rate b = 0.4 (solid line) and b = 0.1 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the two half-maxima, log(2)/b."
x_values = seq(0, 20, length.out = 300)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(saturating_exponential(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.4),
        saturating_exponential(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.1)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.4", "b = 0.1"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("b = 0.4", "b = 0.1"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.5, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log(2) / c(0.4, 0.1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: emergence of seedlings"}

The cumulative number of seedlings that have emerged in a plot approaches 120 seedlings
per m², and 60 seedlings per m² have emerged after 7 days. Find the rate $b$ of a
saturating exponential function with these properties. After how many days have 90% of the
seedlings emerged? What is the rate of emergence at the start?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Half of the asymptote is reached after 7 days, so $\log 2/b=7$ and
$b=\log 2/7\approx0.099$ per day. The function reaches 90% of its asymptote at
$\log(10)/b\approx23.3$ days. The initial slope is $ab=120\times0.099\approx11.9$ seedlings
per m² per day.

:::
::::

## Ricker {#sec-fn-ricker}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * x * exp(-b * x)} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y \leq a/(be) \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{initial slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = 1/b \text{ with value } a/(be);\ \text{inflection point at } x = 2/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\,x\,e^{-x/c} \text{ with } c = 1/b;\quad x\,e^{r(1 - x/K)} \text{ with } a = e^{r},\ b = r/K
\end{aligned}
$$

The Ricker function describes a response that increases in proportion to the predictor
when the predictor is small, reaches a maximum and declines towards zero. Ricker (1954)
proposed it for the number of recruits of a fish stock as a function of the number of
spawners. Its mechanism is a production per individual that declines exponentially with
density, $ae^{-bx}$, so that the total production of $x$ individuals is $axe^{-bx}$. In
fisheries the decline is attributed to competition among the young fish, for example
through cannibalism (Quinn and Deriso 1999), and the same form describes populations in
which fecundity falls with density (Hassell 1975; Royama 1992; Brännström and Sumpter
2005). The function is also used phenomenologically for any response that starts at zero,
peaks and falls. It is one of the two functions of
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd), where its properties are derived.

The function is

$$
f(x)=axe^{-bx},
$$

where $a$ is the initial slope and $b$ is the rate at which the production per individual
declines. Chapter 5 shows that

$$
f'(x)=a(1-bx)\,e^{-bx}, \qquad f''(x)=-ab(2-bx)\,e^{-bx},
$$

which gives a maximum at $x_{\max}=1/b$, with value $a/(be)$, and an
[inflection point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-inflection) at $x=2/b$, where the
value is $2a/(be^2)$ and the decline is steepest. At the maximum the production per
individual is $ae^{-1}$, that is, 37% of what it is at low density.

In population ecology the function is written with a growth rate $r$ and a carrying
capacity $K$,

$$
f(x)=x\,e^{r(1-x/K)},
$$

which is the form above with $a=e^{r}$ and $b=r/K$. In this form $f(K)=K$: at the carrying
capacity the output equals the input. With the location of the peak as a parameter the
function is $axe^{-x/c}$, and the
[generalised Ricker](#sec-fn-generalised-ricker) function takes both the location and the
height of the peak as parameters.

### Example: seed production of an annual grass

Suppose that the number of seeds produced per m² by an annual grass, as a function of the
density of plants $x$ (plants per m²), is $f(x)=120xe^{-0.004x}$. The parameter $a=120$
seeds per plant is the seed production of a plant without neighbours and $b=0.004$ m² per
plant is the rate at which the production per plant declines with density. The seed
production per m² is highest at

$$
x_{\max}=\frac{1}{0.004}=250 \text{ plants per m}^2,
\qquad
f(250)=\frac{120}{0.004\,e}\approx11036 \text{ seeds per m}^2,
$$

where each plant produces $120e^{-1}\approx44$ seeds. The inflection point is at
$2/0.004=500$ plants per m², where the function gives
$2\times120/(0.004e^2)\approx8120$ seeds per m². We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Ricker function: initial slope a and rate b
ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x * exp(-b * x)
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of densities
density_grid = seq(0, 2000, by = 0.01)
seed_values = ricker(density_grid, a = 120, b = 0.004)
density_grid[which.max(seed_values)]
max(seed_values)

# The values derived on paper: 1 / b and a / (b * e)
1 / 0.004
120 / (0.004 * exp(1))

# Value at the inflection point and second derivative there
ricker(x = 500, a = 120, b = 0.004)
ricker_second = D(D(expression(a * x * exp(-b * x)), "x"), "x")
eval(ricker_second, list(a = 120, b = 0.004, x = 500))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Ricker functions with an initial slope a = 120 and a rate b = 0.004 (solid line) and b = 0.008 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the locations of the two maxima, 1/b."
x_values = seq(0, 1500, length.out = 400)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(ricker(x_values, a = 120, b = 0.004), ricker(x_values, a = 120, b = 0.008)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.004", "b = 0.008"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1 / c(0.004, 0.008), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```
