:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: a Ricker function in its population form"}

A paper describes the number of voles in a meadow in one year as a function of their
number $x$ in the previous year with $f(x)=xe^{r(1-x/K)}$, where $r=1.5$ and $K=800$
voles. Write the function as $axe^{-bx}$. At which number of voles is the function
highest, and which value does it have there?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Since $e^{r(1-x/K)}=e^{r}e^{-(r/K)x}$, we have $a=e^{1.5}\approx4.48$ voles per vole and
$b=r/K=1.5/800=0.001875$ per vole. The maximum is at $x_{\max}=1/b=K/r\approx533$ voles,
where the function equals $a/(be)=(K/r)\,e^{r-1}=533\times e^{0.5}\approx879$ voles.

:::
::::

## Logistic {#sec-fn-logistic}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a / (1 + exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, symmetric around its midpoint} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{steepness (inverse units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{midpoint (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/(1 + e^{bc}) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a/2 \text{ and slope } ab/4 \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}} \text{ with } a = 1,\ b = \beta_1,\ c = -\beta_0/\beta_1;\quad
\dfrac{K}{1 + \frac{K - n_0}{n_0}e^{-rx}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The logistic function describes a response that increases from a lower to an upper limit,
slowly at first, fastest half-way and slowly again. In population ecology it is the size
of a population whose growth rate per individual declines linearly with its density,
which is its mechanism (see Adler 2004). With an upper asymptote of 1 it
is the usual function for a probability that changes with a predictor, and in that role it
is phenomenological: it is chosen because it stays between 0 and 1. Verhulst (1838)
proposed the curve as a model for the growth of a population and later gave it its name
(*courbe logistique*).

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{1+e^{-b(x-c)}},
$$

where $a$ is the upper asymptote, $b$ is the steepness and $c$ is the midpoint. The
function is defined for negative values of $x$ as well, so it has two ends. As
$x\to\infty$, $e^{-b(x-c)}\to0$ and $f(x)\to a$. As $x\to-\infty$ the exponential grows
without bound and $f(x)\to0$. So the function has two asymptotes, 0 and $a$. At $x=0$ its
value is $a/(1+e^{bc})$, which is small when $bc$ is large but is never zero.

For the derivative we write $f(x)=a\,u^{-1}$ with $u=1+e^{-b(x-c)}$ and apply the chain
rule:

$$
f'(x)=\frac{ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}}{\left(1+e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^2}=b\,f(x)\left(1-\frac{f(x)}{a}\right),
$$

where the last equality follows from $f(x)/a=1/u$ and $1-f(x)/a=e^{-b(x-c)}/u$. It writes
the slope in terms of the function itself, which is convenient: the slope is close to zero
where $f(x)$ is close to 0 or to $a$, and it is largest in between. If we differentiate
$f'(x)=bf(x)-(b/a)f(x)^2$ once more with the chain rule, we obtain

$$
f''(x)=b\,f'(x)-\frac{2b}{a}\,f(x)\,f'(x)=b\,f'(x)\left(1-\frac{2f(x)}{a}\right).
$$

Since $f'(x)$ is positive everywhere, the second derivative is zero only where
$f(x)=a/2$, which happens at $x=c$ (there the exponential equals $e^{0}=1$). The function
is convex before that point and concave after it. So the midpoint $c$ is the
[inflection point](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-inflection) of the function: the
value of $x$ at which the function reaches half of its asymptote and at which it is
steepest. The slope at the midpoint is $f'(c)=b\,(a/2)(1-1/2)=ab/4$, so for a given
asymptote the parameter $b$ sets the maximum slope. The function is symmetric around its
midpoint: $f(c+s)+f(c-s)=a$ for any distance $s$.

To find where the function reaches a fraction $p$ of its asymptote we solve $f(x_p)=pa$,
which gives $e^{-b(x_p-c)}=(1-p)/p$ and

$$
x_p=c+\frac{1}{b}\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=c+\frac{\operatorname{logit}p}{b}.
$$

So the function reaches 90% of its asymptote at $c+\log(9)/b\approx c+2.2/b$ and 10% at
$c-2.2/b$. The distance between these two points, $4.4/b$, is a convenient way of reading
$b$ from a plot.

The logistic function has three forms that are in common use (see
[Reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation)). The one of this
entry has the upper asymptote, the steepness and the midpoint as parameters. Statistical
texts write the function with an asymptote of 1 as the inverse logit of a straight line,

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta_1x)}}=\frac{e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}}{1+e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x}},
$$

where $\beta_0$ is the intercept and $\beta_1$ the slope of the line. Comparing the
exponents, $\beta_1=b$ and $\beta_0=-bc$, so the midpoint is $c=-\beta_0/\beta_1$. In R
this form is `plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x)`. In population ecology, with time as the input,
the function is written as

$$
f(x)=\frac{K}{1+\dfrac{K-n_0}{n_0}\,e^{-rx}},
$$

where $K$ is the carrying capacity, $n_0$ is the size of the population at $x=0$ and $r$
is its growth rate per individual at low density. In this form the function is the
solution of a differential equation for the growth of a population, $dn/dt=rn(1-n/K)$,
which is where the parameters $r$ and $K$ come from (this book does not work with
dynamical models, so we use the function only as a curve). It is the form of this entry
with $a=K$, $b=r$ and $c=\log\left((K-n_0)/n_0\right)/r$. Some texts write the function
with the hyperbolic tangent, $\tfrac{a}{2}\left[1+\tanh\left(b(x-c)/2\right)\right]$,
which is again the same curve. A lower asymptote other than zero is obtained by adding a
parameter, $d+a/(1+e^{-b(x-c)})$, as in the [threshold](#sec-fn-threshold) entry.

### Example: maturity and body length

Suppose that the probability that a female fish is mature, as a function of her body
length $x$ (cm), is a logistic function with $a=1$, $b=0.25$ per cm and $c=60$ cm. Half of
the females of 60 cm are mature, and around that length the probability increases by
$ab/4=0.0625$ per cm. At 50 cm the probability is

$$
f(50)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-0.25\times(50-60)}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{2.5}}\approx0.076,
$$

and 90% of the females are mature at a length of $60+\log(9)/0.25\approx68.8$ cm. In the
statistical form the function is $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(-15+0.25x)$, since
$\beta_0=-bc=-15$. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Logistic function: upper asymptote a, steepness b and midpoint c
logistic = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a / (1 + exp(-b * (x - c)))
}

# Probability of being mature at 50 and 60 cm
logistic(x = c(50, 60), a = 1, b = 0.25, c = 60)

# The same with plogis() and with the hyperbolic tangent
plogis(-15 + 0.25 * c(50, 60))
0.5 * (1 + tanh(0.25 * (c(50, 60) - 60) / 2))

# Length at which 90% of the females are mature
length_90 = 60 + log(9) / 0.25
length_90
logistic(x = length_90, a = 1, b = 0.25, c = 60)

# Slope at the midpoint: D() and the formula a * b / 4
logistic_derivative = D(expression(a / (1 + exp(-b * (x - c)))), "x")
eval(logistic_derivative, list(a = 1, b = 0.25, c = 60, x = 60))
1 * 0.25 / 4
```

The population form can be checked in the same way, for a population that starts at 1 and
approaches a carrying capacity of 10 with a growth rate of 0.8 per unit of time:

```{r}
# Population form with carrying capacity K = 10, initial size n0 = 1 and rate r = 0.8
x_values = seq(0, 10, by = 2)
10 / (1 + ((10 - 1) / 1) * exp(-0.8 * x_values))

# The same function in midpoint form: a = K, b = r and c = log((K - n0) / n0) / r
logistic(x_values, a = 10, b = 0.8, c = log((10 - 1) / 1) / 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Logistic functions with an upper asymptote a = 1 and a midpoint c = 60, for a steepness b = 0.25 (solid line) and b = 0.1 (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the midpoint and half of the asymptote."
x_values = seq(20, 100, length.out = 300)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(logistic(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.25, c = 60),
        logistic(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.1, c = 60)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.25", "b = 0.1"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("b = 0.25", "b = 0.1"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.5, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: height growth of a tree"}

The height of a tree approaches 30 m. The tree is 15 m tall at an age of 25 years, which is
also when it grows fastest, at 0.9 m per year. Find the parameters $a$, $b$ and $c$ of a
logistic function with these properties, with their units. At which age is the tree 27 m
tall?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The asymptote is $a=30$ m. Half of it is reached at the midpoint, so $c=25$ years, which is
also where the slope is largest. That slope is $ab/4=0.9$ m per year, so
$b=4\times0.9/30=0.12$ per year. A height of 27 m is 90% of the asymptote, which the
function reaches at $c+\log(9)/b=25+2.197/0.12\approx43.3$ years.

:::
::::

## Gompertz {#sec-fn-gompertz}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, asymmetric} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{inflection point (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a\exp\left(-e^{bc}\right) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a/e \text{ and slope } ab/e \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a\exp\left(-d\,e^{-bx}\right) \text{ with } d = e^{bc}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Gompertz function^[The function is named after Gompertz, who proposed in 1825 a law of
human mortality in which the death rate increases exponentially with age over much of
adult life; see Gompertz (1825).] is a sigmoid function like the logistic, with the
difference that it is asymmetric: it leaves its lower limit quickly and approaches its
upper limit slowly. It is used as an alternative to the logistic function for the growth
of organisms and of populations. It can be derived from the assumption that the relative
growth rate, $f'(x)/f(x)$, declines exponentially with $x$, as we show below. The practical
of [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) compares it with the logistic
function.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
$$

where $a$ is the upper asymptote, $b$ is a rate and $c$ is the location of the inflection
point. To analyse it we write $u=e^{-b(x-c)}$, so that $f(x)=ae^{-u}$. As $x\to\infty$,
$u\to0$ and $f(x)\to a$; as $x\to-\infty$, $u$ grows without bound and $f(x)\to0$. The
chain rule, with $du/dx=-bu$, gives

$$
f'(x)=ae^{-u}\times bu=b\,u\,f(x)=b\,f(x)\,\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right),
$$

where the last step uses $u=-\log\left(f(x)/a\right)$. The relative growth rate is
therefore $f'(x)/f(x)=bu=b\,e^{-b(x-c)}$, an exponential decay. Differentiating once more
with the product rule:

$$
f''(x)=b\,f'(x)\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right)-b\,f'(x)
=b\,f'(x)\left[\log\left(\frac{a}{f(x)}\right)-1\right].
$$

Since $f'(x)$ is positive, the second derivative is zero only where $\log(a/f(x))=1$,
that is, where $f(x)=a/e$. This happens when $u=1$, at $x=c$. So the inflection point is
at $x=c$, where the function has reached $1/e\approx37\%$ of its asymptote (against 50%
for the logistic function) and its slope is $ab/e$. Half of the asymptote is reached later,
where $u=\log 2$, at $x=c-\log(\log 2)/b\approx c+0.37/b$.

The function is also written as $a\exp\left(-d\,e^{-bx}\right)$, with $d=e^{bc}$. In that
form the value at zero is $ae^{-d}$ and the inflection point is at $x=\log d/b$.

### Example: growth of a chick

Suppose that the body mass of a tern chick (g) as a function of its age $x$ (days) follows
a Gompertz function with $a=110$ g, $b=0.15$ per day and $c=5$ days. At hatching the chick
weighs

$$
f(0)=110\exp\left(-e^{0.15\times5}\right)=110\exp(-2.117)\approx13.2 \text{ g}.
$$

It grows fastest at an age of 5 days, when it weighs $110/e\approx40.5$ g and gains
$ab/e=110\times0.15/e\approx6.1$ g per day. It reaches half of its final mass at
$5-\log(\log 2)/0.15\approx7.4$ days, and at 20 days it weighs
$110\exp\left(-e^{-2.25}\right)\approx99$ g. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Gompertz function: upper asymptote a, rate b and inflection point c
gompertz = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))
}

# Body mass (g) at hatching, at 5 days and at 20 days
gompertz(x = c(0, 5, 20), a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5)

# Slope at the inflection point: D() and the formula a * b / e
gompertz_derivative = D(expression(a * exp(-exp(-b * (x - c)))), "x")
eval(gompertz_derivative, list(a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5, x = 5))
110 * 0.15 / exp(1)

# The second derivative is zero at the inflection point
gompertz_second = D(gompertz_derivative, "x")
eval(gompertz_second, list(a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5, x = 5))

# Age at which the chick reaches half of its final mass
age_half = 5 - log(log(2)) / 0.15
age_half
gompertz(x = age_half, a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Gompertz function with a = 110, b = 0.15 and c = 5 (solid line) and the logistic function with the same asymptote, the same inflection point and the same maximum slope (dashed line; b = 0.22). Dashed grey lines mark the inflection point and the values a/e and a/2 that the two functions have there."
x_values = seq(-10, 35, length.out = 400)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(gompertz(x_values, a = 110, b = 0.15, c = 5),
        110 / (1 + exp(-(4 * 0.15 / exp(1)) * (x_values - 5)))),
  curve = rep(c("Gompertz", "Logistic"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(110 / exp(1), 55), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: height of a sapling"}

The height of a sapling (cm) as a function of its age $x$ (years) is given as
$80\exp\left(-4e^{-0.5x}\right)$. What is its height at $x=0$? At which age does it grow
fastest, how tall is it then and how fast does it grow?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

This is the second form of the function, with $a=80$ cm, $d=4$ and $b=0.5$ per year. At
$x=0$ the height is $80e^{-4}\approx1.5$ cm. The sapling grows fastest at the inflection
point, $c=\log d/b=\log 4/0.5\approx2.8$ years, when its height is $a/e\approx29.4$ cm and
its growth rate is $ab/e=80\times0.5/e\approx14.7$ cm per year.

:::
::::

## Bell-shaped {#sec-fn-gaussian}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2))| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal, symmetric} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{height of the peak (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{width (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{location of the peak (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty \text{ and as } x \to -\infty \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = c \text{ with value } a;\ \text{inflection points at } x = c \pm b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2} \text{ with } \beta_2 < 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The bell-shaped function, or Gaussian curve, describes a response that is highest at one
value of the predictor and declines symmetrically on both sides of it. It is used for the
abundance or the performance of a species along an environmental gradient, with the
location of the peak as the optimum of the species and the width as its tolerance. It is a
phenomenological function. Its formula is that of the probability density of the
[Normal distribution](distributions.qmd#sec-normal), multiplied by a constant so that the
height of the peak is a parameter; here it describes a curve and the area under it has no
role.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\,e^{-(x-c)^2/(2b^2)},
$$

where $a$ is the height of the peak, $c$ its location and $b$ its width. The parameter $c$
can take any value. The exponent is zero at $x=c$, where $f(c)=a$, and it becomes more and
more negative on both sides, so $f(x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$. The chain
rule gives

$$
f'(x)=-\frac{x-c}{b^2}\,f(x),
\qquad
f''(x)=\left[\frac{(x-c)^2}{b^2}-1\right]\frac{f(x)}{b^2}.
$$

The slope is positive for $x<c$, zero at $x=c$ and negative for $x>c$, so the maximum is
at $c$. The second derivative is zero where $(x-c)^2=b^2$: the inflection points are at
$x=c\pm b$, where the function equals $a\,e^{-1/2}\approx0.61a$. The function is concave
between them and convex outside. If we solve $f(x)=a/2$ we find that the function is at
half of its height at $x=c\pm b\sqrt{2\log 2}\approx c\pm1.18b$.

The logarithm of the function is a parabola, so the function is the exponential of a
quadratic function, $e^{\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2}$ with $\beta_2<0$ (a
[composition](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-composition)). Comparing the two forms
gives

$$
c=-\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}, \qquad b=\sqrt{-\frac{1}{2\beta_2}}, \qquad
a=e^{\beta_0-\beta_1^2/(4\beta_2)}.
$$

For a probability, which cannot exceed 1, the corresponding function is the inverse logit
of a quadratic function, $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left[d-b(x-c)^2\right]$, which is
presented in Chapter 5 and used in the practical of
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Practicals/no_solution.qmd).

### Example: a diatom along a gradient of pH

Suppose that the abundance of a diatom (cells per ml) in lakes of different pH, $x$,
follows a bell-shaped function with $a=200$ cells per ml, $c=6.5$ and $b=0.8$ units of pH.
The abundance is highest, 200 cells per ml, at a pH of 6.5. At the inflection point
$c+b=7.3$ and at a pH of 5 it is

$$
f(7.3)=200\,e^{-1/2}\approx121,
\qquad
f(5)=200\,e^{-(5-6.5)^2/(2\times0.8^2)}=200\,e^{-1.758}\approx34.5
$$

cells per ml. The abundance is at least half of its maximum within
$0.8\sqrt{2\log 2}\approx0.94$ units of pH from the optimum, that is, between a pH of 5.56
and 7.44. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Bell-shaped function: height a, width b and location c of the peak
bell_shaped = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0) {
  a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2))
}

# Abundance (cells per ml) at a pH of 6.5, 7.3 and 5
bell_shaped(x = c(6.5, 7.3, 5), a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5)

# Values of pH at which the abundance is half of its maximum
half_height = 6.5 + c(-1, 1) * 0.8 * sqrt(2 * log(2))
half_height
bell_shaped(x = half_height, a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5)

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection points
# c - b and c + b
bell_expression = expression(a * exp(-(x - c)^2 / (2 * b^2)))
bell_second = D(D(bell_expression, "x"), "x")
eval(bell_second, list(a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5, x = c(5.7, 7.3)))

# The same curve from the Normal density, rescaled to a height of a
200 * 0.8 * sqrt(2 * pi) * dnorm(x = 5, mean = 6.5, sd = 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Bell-shaped functions with a peak of height a = 200 at c = 6.5, for a width b = 0.8 (solid line) and b = 0.4 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the peak and the inflection points c − b and c + b of the solid curve."
x_values = seq(3.5, 9.5, length.out = 400)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(bell_shaped(x_values, a = 200, b = 0.8, c = 6.5),
        bell_shaped(x_values, a = 200, b = 0.4, c = 6.5)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.8", "b = 0.4"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("b = 0.8", "b = 0.4"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5.7, 6.5, 7.3), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: a sedge and the depth of the water table"}

The expected number of shoots of a sedge in a quadrat is described as
$e^{-1+2x-0.25x^2}$, where $x$ is the depth of the water table (dm). Write this function
as a bell-shaped function: at which depth is the expected number highest, how high is it
there, and what is the width $b$?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Here $\beta_0=-1$, $\beta_1=2$ and $\beta_2=-0.25$. The peak is at
$c=-\beta_1/(2\beta_2)=-2/(-0.5)=4$ dm. Its height is
$a=e^{\beta_0-\beta_1^2/(4\beta_2)}=e^{-1+4}=e^{3}\approx20.1$ shoots per quadrat, which is
also what we obtain by evaluating the function at $x=4$: $e^{-1+8-4}=e^{3}$. The width is
$b=\sqrt{-1/(2\beta_2)}=\sqrt{2}\approx1.41$ dm. So the function is
$20.1\,e^{-(x-4)^2/4}$.

:::
::::

# Functions with a power parameter

In the functions of this group a parameter appears as an exponent. An exponent has no
units and changes the shape of a function, which makes these functions flexible. Most of
them contain one of the functions of the previous groups as a special case (see
[Nested functions](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions)).

## Power law {#sec-fn-power}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x^b| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{monotonic: increasing when } b > 0,\ \text{decreasing when } b < 0 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x > 0 \quad (x \geq 0 \text{ when } b > 0) \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y > 0 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{value at } x = 1 \text{ (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x^b\text{)};\quad
b = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } b > 0;\ \text{grows without bound when } b < 0 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } b > 0;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } b < 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{none: multiplying } x \text{ by a factor } m \text{ multiplies } y \text{ by } m^b \text{ everywhere} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \log y = \log a + b\log x;\quad y_0\,(x/x_0)^b \text{ with } y_0 = a\,x_0^b
\end{aligned}
$$

The power law describes a response that changes by a constant proportion when the
predictor changes by a constant proportion. It is the function of allometry, the study of
how the properties of organisms change with their size: the reproductive biomass of plants
as a function of the diameter of their stem (Niklas 1993) and the metabolic rate of
animals as a function of their body mass (Etienne et al. 2006) are two examples. It is
also used for the number of species as a function of the area sampled (Tjørve 2003) and
for the fractal properties of landscapes (Halley et al. 2004). A power law is mechanistic
when it follows from geometry (the surface of an organism is proportional to the square of
its length and its volume to the cube), and many other mechanisms lead to power laws
(Mitzenmacher 2003), so the function alone says little about the process behind it.

The function is

$$
f(x)=ax^{b},
$$

where $b$ is the exponent, which can be positive or negative, and $a$ is the value of the
function at $x=1$. The two ends depend on the sign of $b$. When $b>0$ the function starts
at zero and grows without bound; when $b<0$ it is unbounded as $x\to0$ and tends to zero
as $x\to\infty$. The power rule gives

$$
f'(x)=ab\,x^{b-1}=b\,\frac{f(x)}{x}, \qquad f''(x)=ab(b-1)\,x^{b-2}.
$$

The function is convex when $b>1$ or $b<0$, concave when $0<b<1$ and a straight line
through the origin when $b=1$. Rearranging the first derivative gives

$$
\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{b}{x},
$$

which says that a small relative change in $x$ produces a relative change in $y$ that is
$b$ times as large: an increase of 1% in $x$ changes $y$ by about $b$%. For a change of any
size, $f(mx)=a(mx)^{b}=m^{b}f(x)$, so multiplying $x$ by $m$ multiplies $y$ by $m^{b}$,
whatever the value of $x$. It follows that the power law has no characteristic scale and no
half-maximum. It has no upper asymptote either; when $b<0$ it has a horizontal asymptote at
zero, which it approaches as $x\to\infty$. This is the main difference from the exponential function,
in which it is a fixed step added to $x$ that multiplies $y$ by a constant factor.

Taking logarithms gives $\log f(x)=\log a+b\log x$: on a plot with two logarithmic axes
the power law is a straight line with slope $b$. The
units of $a$ are awkward, since they depend on $b$. They become those of $y$ if we write
the function with a reference value $x_0$ of the predictor,

$$
f(x)=y_0\left(\frac{x}{x_0}\right)^{b}, \qquad y_0=a\,x_0^{b},
$$

where $y_0$ is the value of the function at $x=x_0$.

### Example: species and area

Suppose that the number of plant species found in a sample of grassland of area $x$ (ha)
is $f(x)=12x^{0.25}$. The parameter $a=12$ is the number of species in one hectare and the
exponent is $b=0.25$. In 16 ha and in 10000 ha the function gives

$$
f(16)=12\times16^{0.25}=12\times2=24,
\qquad
f(10000)=12\times10000^{0.25}=12\times10=120
$$

species. Doubling the area multiplies the number of species by $2^{0.25}\approx1.19$, at
any area, and doubling the number of species requires an area that is $2^{1/0.25}=16$
times larger. The slope at 16 ha is $b\,f(16)/16=0.25\times24/16=0.375$ species per ha.
Written around 16 ha, the function is $24(x/16)^{0.25}$. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Power law: value a at x = 1 and exponent b
power_law = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x^b
}

# Number of species in 1, 16 and 10000 ha
power_law(x = c(1, 16, 10000), a = 12, b = 0.25)

# Factor by which the number of species changes when the area doubles
power_law(x = c(2, 32, 20000), a = 12, b = 0.25) / power_law(x = c(1, 16, 10000), a = 12, b = 0.25)

# Slope at 16 ha: D() and the formula b * f(x) / x
power_derivative = D(expression(a * x^b), "x")
eval(power_derivative, list(a = 12, b = 0.25, x = 16))
0.25 * 24 / 16

# The same function written around a reference area of 16 ha, at 100 ha
24 * (100 / 16)^0.25
power_law(x = 100, a = 12, b = 0.25)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Power laws with a = 1 and an exponent b = 0.5 (solid line), b = 1 (dashed line) and b = 2 (dotted line), on the original axes (left) and on logarithmic axes (right), where each of them is a straight line with slope b. The three functions cross at x = 1, where they equal a."
library(patchwork)

x_values = seq(0.1, 3, length.out = 300)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(power_law(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.5), power_law(x_values, a = 1, b = 1),
        power_law(x_values, a = 1, b = 2)),
  curve = rep(c("b = 0.5", "b = 1", "b = 2"), each = length(x_values))
)

panel_original = ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()

panel_log = panel_original +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "x (logarithmic axis)", y = "y (logarithmic axis)")

panel_original + panel_log + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: leaf area and leaf length"}

A leaf that is 5 cm long has an area of 20 cm², and a leaf that is 10 cm long has an area
of 80 cm².
Find the parameters $a$ and $b$ of the power law through these two points. Which area
does it give for a leaf of 15 cm? What does the value of $b$ say about the shape of the
leaves?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Doubling the length multiplies the area by $80/20=4$, so $2^{b}=4$ and $b=2$. In general,
$b=\log(y_2/y_1)/\log(x_2/x_1)$, the slope of the line on logarithmic axes. From the first
point, $a=20/5^{2}=0.8$ cm² per cm², a number without units. For a leaf of 15 cm the
function gives $0.8\times15^{2}=180$ cm². An exponent of 2 means that the area is
proportional to the square of the length, as it is for leaves that keep the same shape as
they become larger; $a=0.8$ is then the area of a leaf as a fraction of the square of its
length.

:::
::::

## von Bertalanffy {#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \texttt{a * (1 - exp(-b * (x - c)))} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating (simple form)};\quad \text{sigmoid (generalised form)} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq c \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{asymptotic size (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{growth rate (inverse units of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{value of } x \text{ at which the size is zero (units of } x\text{)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a\left(1 - e^{bc}\right),\ \text{slope } ab\,e^{bc} \quad (c \leq 0) \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{half of the asymptote at } x = c + \log 2/b \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a - (a - y_0)\,e^{-bx} \text{ with } y_0 = a\left(1 - e^{bc}\right);\quad
a\left(1 - e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^{1/(1-d)} \text{ (generalised form)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The von Bertalanffy function describes the size of an organism as a function of its age.
It is the usual growth curve in fisheries and it is a mechanistic function (von
Bertalanffy 1938): it follows from a balance between the energy that an organism
assimilates and the energy that it spends on maintenance (Essington et al. 2001). In its
simple form, which is used for body length, it is a
[saturating exponential](#sec-fn-monomolecular) function that is shifted along $x$. In its
generalised form, which is used for body mass, the saturating exponential is raised to a
power, and the function becomes sigmoid.

The simple form is

$$
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right),
$$

where $a$ is the asymptotic size, $b$ is the growth rate and $c$ is the age at which the
function is zero. An organism has a positive size at birth, so $c$ is zero or negative
when $x$ is the age since birth: it is where the curve would start if we extended it
backwards, and it is a
[location parameter](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts) with no biological
meaning of its own. The properties are those of the saturating exponential function, moved
by $c$. The size at birth is $f(0)=a\left(1-e^{bc}\right)$, the function tends to $a$ as
$x\to\infty$, and its derivative,

$$
f'(x)=ab\,e^{-b(x-c)}=b\left(a-f(x)\right),
$$

is positive and decreases with age, so growth is fastest at birth and the function is
concave. Half of the asymptotic size is reached at $x=c+\log 2/b$. Since the size at birth
is easier to interpret than $c$, the function is also written as
$a-(a-y_0)\,e^{-bx}$ with $y_0=f(0)$.

The generalised form is

$$
f(x)=a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)^{1/(1-d)},
$$

where $d$ is an exponent between 0 and 1, without units. It is the size of an organism
that gains mass at a rate proportional to its mass raised to the power $d$ and loses mass
at a rate proportional to its mass; the rate $b$ is then $1-d$ times the rate of loss.
With $d=0$ the exponent $1/(1-d)$ is 1 and we recover the simple form, so the simple form
is [nested](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions) in the generalised one. The
value $d=2/3$ is often used, on the argument that assimilation is proportional to a
surface (a length squared) and mass to a volume (a length cubed) (Quinn and Deriso 1999).
The exponent is then 3, and the function is the cube of the simple form: if length follows
the simple form and mass is proportional to the cube of length, mass follows the
generalised form with $d=2/3$ and the same $b$ and $c$.

To find the landmarks of the generalised form we write $m=1/(1-d)$ and
$u=e^{-b(x-c)}$, so that $f(x)=a(1-u)^m$ and $du/dx=-bu$. The chain rule and then the
product rule give

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= abm\,u\,(1-u)^{m-1}, \\
f''(x) &= -ab^2m\,u\,(1-u)^{m-2}\left(1-mu\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

For $m>1$ the slope is zero at $x=c$, where $u=1$, and the second derivative changes sign
where $u=1/m$. So the generalised form has an inflection point at

$$
x=c+\frac{\log m}{b}, \qquad \text{with value } a\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)^{m}=a\,d^{\,1/(1-d)}.
$$

For $d=2/3$ the inflection point is at $c+\log 3/b$, where the function equals
$(2/3)^3a=8a/27\approx0.30\,a$: an organism that follows this function gains mass fastest
when it has reached 30% of its final mass.

### Example: length and mass of a turtle

Suppose that the length of the carapace of a turtle (cm) as a function of its age $x$
(years) follows the simple form with $a=30$ cm, $b=0.12$ per year and $c=-1.5$ years. At
hatching and at an age of 10 years the carapace is

$$
f(0)=30\left(1-e^{0.12\times(-1.5)}\right)=30\left(1-e^{-0.18}\right)\approx4.9 \text{ cm},
\qquad
f(10)=30\left(1-e^{-0.12\times11.5}\right)\approx22.5 \text{ cm}
$$

long. A hatchling grows by $ab\,e^{bc}=3.6\,e^{-0.18}\approx3.0$ cm per year, and the
turtle reaches half of its final length at $-1.5+\log 2/0.12\approx4.3$ years.

Suppose also that the body mass of the turtle is proportional to the cube of the length
of its carapace and approaches 2500 g. Body mass then follows the generalised form with
$a=2500$ g, $d=2/3$ and the same $b$ and $c$. At 10 years the turtle weighs
$2500\times(22.5/30)^3\approx1048$ g. It gains mass fastest at an age of
$-1.5+\log 3/0.12\approx7.7$ years, when it weighs $8\times2500/27\approx741$ g. We can
verify our math with R:

```{r}
# von Bertalanffy function: asymptotic size a, growth rate b, age c at which the size
# is zero and exponent d (d = 0 gives the simple form)
von_bertalanffy = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0, d = 0) {
  a * (1 - exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / (1 - d))
}

# Length of the carapace (cm) at hatching and at 10 years
von_bertalanffy(x = c(0, 10), a = 30, b = 0.12, c = -1.5)

# The same written with the length at hatching
30 - (30 - 30 * (1 - exp(-0.18))) * exp(-0.12 * c(0, 10))

# Growth of a hatchling (cm per year) and age at half of the final length
30 * 0.12 * exp(0.12 * -1.5)
-1.5 + log(2) / 0.12

# Body mass (g) at 10 years, with d = 2/3
von_bertalanffy(x = 10, a = 2500, b = 0.12, c = -1.5, d = 2 / 3)

# Age and body mass at the inflection point
age_inflection = -1.5 + log(3) / 0.12
age_inflection
von_bertalanffy(x = age_inflection, a = 2500, b = 0.12, c = -1.5, d = 2 / 3)
8 * 2500 / 27
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "von Bertalanffy functions with b = 0.12 and c = −1.5, as a fraction of the asymptote a: the simple form (solid line; d = 0) and the generalised form with d = 2/3 (dashed line). Dashed grey lines mark the inflection point of the generalised form, c + log(3)/b, and its value there, 8/27 of the asymptote."
x_values = seq(0, 40, length.out = 400)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 2),
  y = c(von_bertalanffy(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.12, c = -1.5),
        von_bertalanffy(x_values, a = 1, b = 0.12, c = -1.5, d = 2 / 3)),
  curve = rep(c("d = 0", "d = 2/3"), each = length(x_values))
)

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 8 / 27, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1.5 + log(3) / 0.12, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  expand_limits(y = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y / a", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: length of a lizard"}

A paper gives the length of a lizard (cm, from snout to vent) as a function of its age $x$
(years) as $12-(12-3)\,e^{-0.4x}$. Find the parameters $a$, $b$ and $c$ of the simple von
Bertalanffy function, with their units. At which age does the lizard reach 90% of its
final length?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The function is written with the length at hatching, $y_0=3$ cm, so $a=12$ cm and $b=0.4$
per year. The parameter $c$ follows from $y_0=a\left(1-e^{bc}\right)$: $e^{0.4c}=1-3/12=0.75$,
so $c=\log(0.75)/0.4\approx-0.72$ years. The function reaches 90% of its asymptote when
$e^{-b(x-c)}=0.1$, that is, at $x=c+\log(10)/b\approx-0.72+5.76=5.04$ years.

:::
::::

## Shepherd {#sec-fn-shepherd}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x / (b + x^c)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{increasing when } c < 1;\ \text{saturating when } c = 1;\ \text{unimodal when } c > 1 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a \text{ (units of } y \text{ times units of } x^{c-1}\text{)};\quad
b \text{ (units of } x^c\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } c < 1;\ f(x) \to a \text{ when } c = 1;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } c > 1 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c > 1,\ \text{maximum at } x = \left(b/(c-1)\right)^{1/c} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{sx}{1 + (x/k)^c},\ \text{with } s = a/b \text{ and } k = b^{1/c}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Shepherd function is a [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function in which
the $x$ of the denominator is raised to a power. It is used for the output of a population
(recruits, seeds, the adults of the next generation) as a function of its density, when
the strength of the competition among individuals is to be estimated from the data
(Maynard Smith and Slatkin 1973; Brännström and Sumpter 2005). The exponent $c$ sets that
strength. With $c=1$ the function is the Michaelis–Menten function and the output levels
off. With $c<1$ the output keeps increasing with density, and with $c>1$ it declines at
high density, as it does for the [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) function; population ecologists
call the two cases undercompensating and overcompensating density dependence. In
fisheries the function generalises the Beverton–Holt curve, and it can be derived from a
mortality of the young fish that depends on the initial size of their cohort (Quinn and
Deriso 1999).

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x^{c}},
$$

where $c$ is the exponent and $a$ and $b$ are positive. The units of $a$ and $b$ depend on
$c$, which makes them hard to interpret, so we first look for landmarks. For small $x$
the term $x^c$ is negligible next to $b$ and $f(x)\approx(a/b)\,x$: the initial slope is
$a/b$. For large $x$ the term $b$ is negligible next to $x^c$ and $f(x)\approx ax^{1-c}$,
which grows without bound when $c<1$, equals $a$ when $c=1$ and tends to zero when $c>1$.
The quotient rule gives

$$
f'(x)=\frac{a\left(b+x^{c}\right)-ax\times cx^{c-1}}{\left(b+x^{c}\right)^2}
=\frac{a\left[b-(c-1)\,x^{c}\right]}{\left(b+x^{c}\right)^2}.
$$

When $c\le1$ the numerator is positive for every $x$ and the function increases
throughout. When $c>1$ the numerator is zero where $x^c=b/(c-1)$, so the function has a
maximum at

$$
x_{\max}=\left(\frac{b}{c-1}\right)^{1/c},
\qquad
f(x_{\max})=\frac{a\,(c-1)}{bc}\,x_{\max},
$$

where the value follows from replacing $x^c$ by $b/(c-1)$ in the denominator.

The function is easier to read with the initial slope $s=a/b$ and the scale $k=b^{1/c}$
as parameters, which we obtain by dividing the numerator and the denominator by $b$:

$$
f(x)=\frac{sx}{1+(x/k)^{c}}.
$$

In this [reparameterisation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-reparameterisation) $k$ has the
units of $x$ and $s$ those of $y$ per unit of $x$. At $x=k$ the denominator equals 2
whatever the value of $c$, so $k$ is the density at which the output is half of what the
initial slope alone would give, $sk/2$. The exponent then decides what happens beyond
$k$, and the maximum for $c>1$ is at $k\,(c-1)^{-1/c}$.

### Example: flour beetles in a jar

Suppose that the number of adult beetles that emerge from a jar of flour, as a function of
the number of eggs $x$ that were laid in it, is $f(x)=8000x/(10000+x^2)$, a Shepherd
function with $c=2$. The initial slope is $a/b=0.8$ adults per egg, the fraction of the
eggs that become adults when there is no competition, and the scale is
$k=\sqrt{10000}=100$ eggs. The number of adults is highest at

$$
x_{\max}=\left(\frac{10000}{2-1}\right)^{1/2}=100 \text{ eggs},
\qquad
f(100)=\frac{8000\times100}{10000+10000}=40 \text{ adults},
$$

which is $sk/2=0.8\times100/2$. With 300 eggs the jar produces
$8000\times300/(10000+90000)=24$ adults. With $c=1$ and the same initial slope and scale
the function is the Michaelis–Menten function $80x/(100+x)$, which gives 40 adults for
100 eggs as well and 60 adults for 300 eggs. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Shepherd function: parameters a and b and exponent c
shepherd = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x^c)
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of numbers of eggs
egg_grid = seq(0, 1000, by = 0.01)
adult_values = shepherd(egg_grid, a = 8000, b = 10000, c = 2)
egg_grid[which.max(adult_values)]
max(adult_values)

# Adults from 100 and from 300 eggs
shepherd(x = c(100, 300), a = 8000, b = 10000, c = 2)

# The same function written with the initial slope s = 0.8 and the scale k = 100
0.8 * c(100, 300) / (1 + (c(100, 300) / 100)^2)

# With c = 1 it is a Michaelis–Menten function with asymptote 80 and half-maximum 100
shepherd(x = c(100, 300), a = 80, b = 100, c = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Shepherd functions with an initial slope s = 0.8 and a scale k = 100, for c = 0.5 (dotted line), c = 1 (dashed line; a Michaelis–Menten function) and c = 2 (solid line). Dashed grey lines mark the scale k and the value sk/2 = 40 that the three functions have there."
x_values = seq(0, 600, length.out = 600)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(shepherd(x_values, a = 0.8 * 100^2, b = 100^2, c = 2),
        shepherd(x_values, a = 0.8 * 100, b = 100, c = 1),
        shepherd(x_values, a = 0.8 * 100^0.5, b = 100^0.5, c = 0.5)),
  curve = rep(c("c = 2", "c = 1", "c = 0.5"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("c = 2", "c = 1", "c = 0.5"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 40, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: biomass of a crop and sowing density"}

The biomass of a crop (kg per m²) as a function of the density at which it was sown, $x$
(thousands of seeds per m²), is described by $f(x)=24x/(16+x^3)$. What is the initial
slope of this Shepherd function? At which sowing density is the biomass highest, and how
high is it there? What does the function do at very high densities?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The initial slope is $a/b=24/16=1.5$ kg per thousand seeds. The exponent is $c=3$, which
is larger than 1, so the function has a maximum at
$x_{\max}=\left(b/(c-1)\right)^{1/c}=(16/2)^{1/3}=2$ thousand seeds per m², where it
equals $24\times2/(16+8)=2$ kg per m². For large $x$ the function is close to
$ax^{1-c}=24/x^2$, so the biomass tends to zero at very high densities.

:::
::::

## Hassell {#sec-fn-hassell}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * x / (b + x)^c| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{increasing when } c < 1;\ \text{saturating when } c = 1;\ \text{unimodal when } c > 1 \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad y \geq 0;\quad 0 \leq y < a \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a \text{ (units of } y \text{ times units of } x^{c-1}\text{)};\quad
b \text{ (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } a/b^c \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad \text{grows without bound when } c < 1;\ f(x) \to a \text{ when } c = 1;\ f(x) \to 0 \text{ when } c > 1 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{when } c > 1,\ \text{maximum at } x = b/(c-1) \text{ and inflection point at } x = 2b/(c-1) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \dfrac{sx}{(1 + x/b)^c},\ \text{with } s = a/b^c \text{ the initial slope}
\end{aligned}
$$

The Hassell function is a [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function in which
the whole denominator is raised to a power. Hassell (1975) proposed it for the density
dependence of populations with one generation per year, and it is used in the same way as
the [Shepherd](#sec-fn-shepherd) function, from which it differs in where the exponent is
placed (see also Brännström and Sumpter 2005). The exponent $c$ again sets the strength of
the competition: the output keeps increasing with density when $c<1$, levels off when
$c=1$ and declines at high density when $c>1$. The function is mostly used
phenomenologically, to let the data decide among these three cases.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{ax}{(b+x)^{c}},
$$

where $c$ is the exponent, $b$ has the units of $x$ and $a$ has units that depend on $c$.
For small $x$ the denominator is close to $b^c$, so the initial slope is $a/b^c$. For
large $x$ the denominator is close to $x^c$ and $f(x)\approx ax^{1-c}$, which gives the
same three cases as for the Shepherd function. The quotient rule, with the chain rule for
the denominator, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= \frac{a\,(b+x)^{c}-ax\times c\,(b+x)^{c-1}}{(b+x)^{2c}}
=\frac{a\left[b-(c-1)\,x\right]}{(b+x)^{c+1}}, \\
f''(x) &= \frac{ac\left[(c-1)\,x-2b\right]}{(b+x)^{c+2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

When $c\le1$ the slope is positive for every $x$. When $c>1$ the numerator of the first
derivative is zero at

$$
x_{\max}=\frac{b}{c-1},
\qquad
f(x_{\max})=\frac{a\,(c-1)^{c-1}}{c^{\,c}\,b^{\,c-1}},
$$

which is a maximum, and the numerator of the second derivative is zero at $x=2b/(c-1)$,
an inflection point on the way down. As for the Ricker function, the inflection point is
at twice the location of the maximum. The value of the maximum follows from
$b+x_{\max}=bc/(c-1)$; for $c=2$ it is $a/(4b)$ and for $c=3$ it is $4a/(27b^2)$.

The resemblance to the Ricker function has a reason. With the initial slope as a
parameter the function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{sx}{(1+x/b)^{c}}, \qquad s=\frac{a}{b^{c}},
$$

and if we let $c$ grow while we keep the ratio $c/b$ at a fixed value $\beta$, the term
$(1+\beta x/c)^{-c}$ tends to $e^{-\beta x}$. So the Hassell function has the
Michaelis–Menten function at one end of its range ($c=1$) and approaches the Ricker
function $sxe^{-\beta x}$ at the other.

### Example: larvae that compete for food

Suppose that the number of adult flies that emerge per gram of food, as a function of the
density of larvae $x$ (larvae per gram), is $f(x)=800x/(10+x)^3$. The exponent is $c=3$
and $b=10$ larvae per gram. The initial slope is $a/b^c=800/1000=0.8$ adults per larva.
The number of adults is highest at

$$
x_{\max}=\frac{10}{3-1}=5 \text{ larvae per gram},
\qquad
f(5)=\frac{800\times5}{15^3}=\frac{4\times800}{27\times10^2}\approx1.19 \text{ adults per gram},
$$

and the inflection point is at $2\times10/(3-1)=10$ larvae per gram, where the function
gives $800\times10/20^3=1$ adult per gram. At 40 larvae per gram it gives
$800\times40/50^3\approx0.26$ adults per gram. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Hassell function: parameters a and b and exponent c
hassell = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x)^c
}

# Location and height of the maximum on a fine grid of densities
larva_grid = seq(0, 200, by = 0.001)
adult_values = hassell(larva_grid, a = 800, b = 10, c = 3)
larva_grid[which.max(adult_values)]
max(adult_values)

# Adults per gram at 5, 10 and 40 larvae per gram
hassell(x = c(5, 10, 40), a = 800, b = 10, c = 3)

# Initial slope: D() and the formula a / b^c
hassell_derivative = D(expression(a * x / (b + x)^c), "x")
eval(hassell_derivative, list(a = 800, b = 10, c = 3, x = 0))
800 / 10^3

# The second derivative is zero at the inflection point
eval(D(hassell_derivative, "x"), list(a = 800, b = 10, c = 3, x = 10))

# With a larger exponent and the same c / b = 0.3 and initial slope, the function
# approaches the Ricker function 0.8 * x * exp(-0.3 * x): values at 5 larvae per gram
0.8 * 5 / (1 + 0.3 * 5 / c(3, 30, 3000))^c(3, 30, 3000)
0.8 * 5 * exp(-0.3 * 5)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Hassell functions with an initial slope s = 0.8 and a ratio c/b = 0.3, for c = 3 (solid line; b = 10) and c = 30 (dashed line; b = 100), and the Ricker function with the same initial slope and a rate of 0.3 (dotted line), which the Hassell function approaches as c grows. Dashed grey lines mark the maximum and the inflection point of the solid curve, at b/(c − 1) = 5 and 2b/(c − 1) = 10."
x_values = seq(0, 40, length.out = 400)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(hassell(x_values, a = 0.8 * 10^3, b = 10, c = 3),
        hassell(x_values, a = 0.8 * 100^30, b = 100, c = 30),
        0.8 * x_values * exp(-0.3 * x_values)),
  curve = rep(c("Hassell, c = 3", "Hassell, c = 30", "Ricker"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve,
                          levels = c("Hassell, c = 3", "Hassell, c = 30", "Ricker"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(5, 10), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: a Hassell function with a given initial slope"}

A Hassell function has $b=12$ plants per m² and $c=4$. Where are its maximum and its
inflection point? Which value of $a$ gives an initial slope of 0.5 seeds per plant, and
how high is the maximum then?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The maximum is at $b/(c-1)=12/3=4$ plants per m² and the inflection point at twice that
density, $2b/(c-1)=8$ plants per m². The initial slope is $a/b^c$, so
$a=0.5\times12^4=10368$. The maximum is then
$f(4)=10368\times4/16^4=41472/65536\approx0.63$ seeds per m², which is also what the
formula gives: $a\,(c-1)^{c-1}/(c^{\,c}b^{\,c-1})=10368\times27/(256\times1728)\approx0.63$.

:::
::::

## Generalised Ricker {#sec-fn-generalised-ricker}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{unimodal, of adjustable width} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y \leq a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{height of the peak (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{location of the peak (units of } x\text{)};\quad c = \text{exponent (no units)} \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0;\ \text{slope } 0 \text{ when } c > 1,\ ae/b \text{ when } c = 1 \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to 0,\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{maximum at } x = b \text{ with value } a;\ \text{inflection points at } x = b\left(1 \pm 1/\sqrt{c}\right) \text{ (only the upper one when } c \leq 1\text{)} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad a'x^{c}e^{-cx/b} \text{ with } a' = a\,(e/b)^{c};\quad
\text{with } c = 1,\ \text{the Ricker function } (ae/b)\,x\,e^{-x/b}
\end{aligned}
$$

The generalised Ricker function describes a response with a single peak whose location,
height and width are three separate parameters. In the [Ricker](#sec-fn-ricker) function
one parameter controls both where the peak is and how fast the function declines beyond
it, so a peak that is far from zero is necessarily wide; the exponent of the generalised
function removes that link. Persson et al. (1998) used it for the attack rate of a
predator as a function of its body mass, and in fisheries it has been proposed for the
number of recruits as a function of the size of the spawning stock (Quinn and Deriso
1999). It is a phenomenological function. [Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions)
uses it for the number of tadpoles killed as a function of their body length. Bellows
(1981) proposed another generalisation of the Ricker function, in which the power is
placed inside the exponential.

The function is

$$
f(x)=a\left[\frac{x}{b}\,e^{1-x/b}\right]^{c},
$$

where $a$ is the height of the peak, $b$ is its location and $c$ is a positive exponent.
The term in brackets is a Ricker function that is written so that its maximum is at
$x=b$ and has a value of 1. The function is zero at $x=0$, and it tends to zero as
$x\to\infty$ because the exponential dominates the power of $x$. The derivative is easiest
to find from the logarithm of the function,
$\log f(x)=\log a+c\left[\log(x/b)+1-x/b\right]$, whose derivative is $f'(x)/f(x)$:

$$
f'(x)=c\,f(x)\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{b}\right).
$$

The slope is positive for $x<b$, zero at $x=b$ and negative for $x>b$, whatever the value
of $c$: the maximum is at $x=b$, where the term in brackets equals 1 and $f(b)=a$.
Differentiating once more with the product rule gives

$$
f''(x)=c\,f(x)\left[c\left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right],
$$

which is zero where $\sqrt{c}\,\left|1-x/b\right|=1$. So the inflection points are at

$$
x=b\left(1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}\right),
$$

one on each side of the peak when $c>1$. The distance between them, $2b/\sqrt{c}$, is a
measure of the width of the peak: a peak that is half as wide needs an exponent that is
four times as large. When $c\le1$ the lower value is zero or negative and is not an
inflection point (with $c=1$ it is $x=0$, where the second derivative is $-2ae/b^2$ and
not zero), so the only inflection point is the upper one. With $c=1$ it is at $2b$, as for
the Ricker function. Near its peak the function is close to the
[bell-shaped](#sec-fn-gaussian) function with height $a$, location $b$ and width
$b/\sqrt{c}$.

With $c=1$ the function is $(ae/b)\,xe^{-x/b}$, a Ricker function with an initial slope
$ae/b$ and a rate $1/b$. For any $c$ the function can be multiplied out to
$a'x^{c}e^{-cx/b}$ with $a'=a\,(e/b)^{c}$, a power of $x$ multiplied by an exponential,
which is the form in which it is often printed.

### Example: attack rate and body mass of a perch

Suppose that the volume of water that a perch clears of zooplankton (litres per hour), as
a function of its body mass $x$ (g), follows a generalised Ricker function with $a=3$
litres per hour, $b=20$ g and $c=4$. The attack rate is highest, 3 litres per hour, for a
perch of 20 g. The inflection points are at $20\,(1\pm1/\sqrt{4})$, that is, at 10 and 30
g, where the function gives

$$
f(10)=3\left[0.5\,e^{0.5}\right]^{4}\approx1.39,
\qquad
f(30)=3\left[1.5\,e^{-0.5}\right]^{4}\approx2.06
$$

litres per hour. The function is asymmetric: it rises more steeply than it falls. With
$c=1$ and the same $a$ and $b$ it would be the Ricker function with an initial slope
$ae/b\approx0.41$ litres per hour per g, which gives 2.47 litres per hour at 10 g and
2.73 at 30 g, a much wider peak. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Generalised Ricker function: height a and location b of the peak, exponent c
generalised_ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1) {
  a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c
}

# Attack rate (litres per hour) at 10, 20 and 30 g
generalised_ricker(x = c(10, 20, 30), a = 3, b = 20, c = 4)

# Location of the maximum on a fine grid of body mass
mass_grid = seq(0, 100, by = 0.001)
mass_grid[which.max(generalised_ricker(mass_grid, a = 3, b = 20, c = 4))]

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection points
ricker_expression = expression(a * ((x / b) * exp(1 - x / b))^c)
ricker_second = D(D(ricker_expression, "x"), "x")
eval(ricker_second, list(a = 3, b = 20, c = 4, x = c(10, 30)))

# With c = 1 it is a Ricker function with initial slope a * e / b and rate 1 / b
generalised_ricker(x = c(10, 30), a = 3, b = 20, c = 1)
(3 * exp(1) / 20) * c(10, 30) * exp(-c(10, 30) / 20)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Generalised Ricker functions with a peak of height a = 3 at b = 20, for an exponent c = 1 (dotted line; a Ricker function), c = 4 (solid line) and c = 16 (dashed line). Vertical dashed lines mark the peak and the inflection points of the solid curve, at 10 and 30."
x_values = seq(0, 80, length.out = 500)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(generalised_ricker(x_values, a = 3, b = 20, c = 4),
        generalised_ricker(x_values, a = 3, b = 20, c = 16),
        generalised_ricker(x_values, a = 3, b = 20, c = 1)),
  curve = rep(c("c = 4", "c = 16", "c = 1"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("c = 4", "c = 16", "c = 1"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(10, 20, 30), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: reading the exponent from a plot"}

The activity of a ground beetle (captures per trap per night) as a function of temperature
is highest at 15 °C, where it is 50 captures, and a plot of the data suggests that the
curve changes from convex to concave at 12 °C and back to convex at 18 °C. Find the
parameters $a$, $b$ and $c$ of a generalised Ricker function with these properties.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The height of the peak is $a=50$ captures per trap per night and its location is $b=15$
°C. The two values at which the curvature changes are the inflection points,
$b\,(1\pm1/\sqrt{c})$. Their distance from the peak is $b/\sqrt{c}=3$ °C, so
$\sqrt{c}=15/3=5$ and $c=25$. These are the values that we would use as starting values
when fitting the function to the data (see
[Starting values by eye](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-starting-values)).

:::
::::

## Non-rectangular hyperbola {#sec-fn-nonrectangular}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|(s + p_max - sqrt((s + p_max)^2 - 4 * theta * s * p_max)) / (2 * theta)|,\ \text{with } \texttt{s = alpha * x} \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{saturating, with a bend of adjustable sharpness} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad x \geq 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 \leq y < p_{\max} \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad \alpha = \text{initial slope (units of } y \text{ per unit of } x\text{)};\quad
p_{\max} = \text{asymptote (units of } y\text{)}; \\
&\quad \theta = \text{sharpness of the bend (no units)},\ 0 < \theta \leq 1 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = 0,\ \text{slope } \alpha \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to p_{\max},\ \text{slope} \to 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{at } x = p_{\max}/\alpha \text{ the function equals } p_{\max}/\left(1 + \sqrt{1 - \theta}\right) \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{the smaller root } y \text{ of } \theta y^2 - (\alpha x + p_{\max})\,y + \alpha x\,p_{\max} = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The non-rectangular hyperbola describes the rate of photosynthesis of a leaf as a function
of the light that it receives. It is a saturating function with three parameters: the
initial slope, the asymptote and the sharpness of the bend between the two. It is derived
from principles of plant physiology (Thornley 2002), so it is a mechanistic function, and
its parameters have their own symbols in that field: $\alpha$ is the efficiency with which
the leaf uses light when light is scarce, $p_{\max}$ is the rate of photosynthesis when
light is abundant and $\theta$ is the sharpness. We keep these symbols here. In the terms
of the [Michaelis–Menten](#sec-fn-michaelis-menten) function, $p_{\max}$ is the asymptote
$a$ and $\alpha$ is the initial slope $a/b$.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{\alpha x+p_{\max}-\sqrt{\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)^2-4\,\theta\,\alpha x\,p_{\max}}}{2\,\theta},
$$

where $x$ is the light received by the leaf. The formula is the smaller of the two
solutions of a quadratic equation in $y=f(x)$,

$$
\theta\,y^2-\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)y+\alpha x\,p_{\max}=0,
$$

and the properties of the function are easier to derive from this equation than from the
formula. If we move the term $(1-\theta)\,y^2$ to the right-hand side, the left-hand side
can be factorised:

$$
\left(\alpha x-y\right)\left(p_{\max}-y\right)=(1-\theta)\,y^2 .
$$

The two factors on the left are the distances from $y$ to the straight line $\alpha x$ and
to the plateau $p_{\max}$. This form shows the two extremes of the function. When
$\theta=1$ the right-hand side is zero, so one of the two factors has to be zero: $y$ is
either on the line or on the plateau, and the smaller root is $\min(\alpha x,p_{\max})$, a
[hockey stick](#sec-fn-hockey-stick) function with a breakpoint at $x=p_{\max}/\alpha$.
When $\theta=0$ the quadratic term of the equation vanishes and what remains is
$\alpha x\,p_{\max}=\left(\alpha x+p_{\max}\right)y$, that is,

$$
y=\frac{\alpha x\,p_{\max}}{\alpha x+p_{\max}}=\frac{p_{\max}\,x}{p_{\max}/\alpha+x},
$$

a Michaelis–Menten function with an asymptote $p_{\max}$ and a half-maximum
$p_{\max}/\alpha$. (The formula itself cannot be evaluated at $\theta=0$, as it divides by
zero; the Michaelis–Menten function is its limit as $\theta\to0$.) Both functions are
therefore [nested](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-nested-functions) in the non-rectangular
hyperbola, and values of $\theta$ between 0 and 1 give curves between them.

The limits follow from the same form. At $x=0$ the equation is satisfied by $y=0$. For
small $x$ and $y$, the term $y^2$ is negligible and $p_{\max}-y\approx p_{\max}$, so
$y\approx\alpha x$: the initial slope is $\alpha$ for every $\theta$. Dividing both sides
by $\alpha x$ gives $(1-y/(\alpha x))(p_{\max}-y)=(1-\theta)\,y^2/(\alpha x)$, whose
right-hand side tends to zero as $x\to\infty$ since $y$ stays below $p_{\max}$, so
$f(x)\to p_{\max}$.

The parameter $\theta$ can be read at one particular value of $x$. At $x=p_{\max}/\alpha$,
where the line $\alpha x$ crosses the plateau, the equation becomes
$\theta y^2-2p_{\max}\,y+p_{\max}^2=0$, and its smaller root is

$$
f\left(\frac{p_{\max}}{\alpha}\right)=\frac{p_{\max}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)}{\theta}
=\frac{p_{\max}}{1+\sqrt{1-\theta}} .
$$

At this value of $x$ the function is at half of its asymptote when $\theta=0$, at two
thirds when $\theta=0.75$ and on the asymptote when $\theta=1$. The sharpness is hard to
estimate from data (Thornley 2002), because it only affects the function around the bend.

Leaves also respire, so that their net exchange of carbon dioxide is negative in the dark.
This is described by subtracting the rate of respiration from the function, which is a
[shift along $y$](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-function-shifts).

### Example: photosynthesis of a leaf

Suppose that a leaf has $\alpha=0.05$ µmol of carbon dioxide per µmol of light,
$p_{\max}=20$ µmol per m² per second and $\theta=0.75$, with the light $x$ in µmol per m²
per second. The line and the plateau cross at $x=p_{\max}/\alpha=20/0.05=400$ µmol per m²
per second, where the rate of photosynthesis is

$$
f(400)=\frac{20}{1+\sqrt{1-0.75}}=\frac{20}{1.5}\approx13.3 \text{ µmol per m}^2 \text{ per second}.
$$

At $x=100$ we have $\alpha x=5$, and the formula gives

$$
f(100)=\frac{5+20-\sqrt{25^2-4\times0.75\times5\times20}}{2\times0.75}
=\frac{25-\sqrt{325}}{1.5}\approx4.65 \text{ µmol per m}^2 \text{ per second},
$$

which lies between the 4 µmol per m² per second of the Michaelis–Menten function
($5\times20/25$) and the 5 of the hockey stick. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Non-rectangular hyperbola: initial slope alpha, asymptote p_max and sharpness theta
non_rectangular = function(x, alpha = 1, p_max = 1, theta = 0.5) {
  (alpha * x + p_max - sqrt((alpha * x + p_max)^2 - 4 * theta * alpha * x * p_max)) /
    (2 * theta)
}

# Photosynthesis at a light of 100, 400 and 1500
light_values = c(100, 400, 1500)
non_rectangular(x = light_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.75)

# Value at x = p_max / alpha from the formula derived on paper
20 / (1 + sqrt(1 - 0.75))

# A sharpness close to 0 gives the Michaelis–Menten function
non_rectangular(x = light_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.000001)
20 * light_values / (20 / 0.05 + light_values)

# A sharpness of 1 gives the hockey stick function
non_rectangular(x = light_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 1)
pmin(0.05 * light_values, 20)

# Initial slope: finite-difference slope at zero with a small step
(non_rectangular(x = 0.001, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.75) - 0) / 0.001
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Non-rectangular hyperbolas with an initial slope α = 0.05 and an asymptote p_max = 20, for a sharpness θ close to 0 (dotted line; a Michaelis–Menten function), θ = 0.75 (solid line) and θ = 1 (dashed line; a hockey stick function). Dashed grey lines mark the asymptote and the value of x at which the line αx crosses it, p_max/α = 400."
x_values = seq(0, 1600, length.out = 801)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(non_rectangular(x_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.75),
        non_rectangular(x_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 1),
        non_rectangular(x_values, alpha = 0.05, p_max = 20, theta = 0.000001)),
  curve = rep(c("theta = 0.75", "theta = 1", "theta close to 0"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve,
                          levels = c("theta = 0.75", "theta = 1", "theta close to 0"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 400, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: the sharpness of a light response"}

The photosynthesis of a leaf approaches 30 µmol per m² per second in bright light and
increases by 0.06 µmol of carbon dioxide per µmol of light when light is scarce. At which
light does the straight line of the initial slope cross the asymptote? At that light the
leaf is measured to photosynthesise at 80% of its asymptote. Which sharpness $\theta$
does this correspond to?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The line crosses the asymptote at $x=p_{\max}/\alpha=30/0.06=500$ µmol per m² per second.
There the function equals $p_{\max}/\left(1+\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)$, so
$1/\left(1+\sqrt{1-\theta}\right)=0.8$. This gives $\sqrt{1-\theta}=1/0.8-1=0.25$ and
$\theta=1-0.25^2=0.9375$. A Michaelis–Menten function would be at 50% of its asymptote at
this light and a hockey stick function at 100%.

:::
::::

## Richards {#sec-fn-richards}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{R}: &\quad \verb|a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)| \\
\text{Shape}: &\quad \text{sigmoid, of adjustable asymmetry} \\
\text{Domain}: &\quad \text{all } x \text{ when } d > 0;\quad x \geq c + \log(-d)/b \text{ when } -1 \leq d < 0 \\
\text{Range}: &\quad 0 < y < a \\
\text{Parameters}: &\quad a = \text{upper asymptote (units of } y\text{)};\quad
b = \text{rate (inverse units of } x\text{)}; \\
&\quad c = \text{inflection point (units of } x\text{)};\quad d = \text{shape (no units)},\ d \geq -1,\ d \neq 0 \\
\text{At zero}: &\quad f(0) = a/\left(1 + d\,e^{bc}\right)^{1/d} \\
\text{At infinity}: &\quad f(x) \to a \text{ as } x \to \infty;\quad f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to -\infty \text{ when } d > 0 \\
\text{Special}: &\quad \text{inflection point at } x = c,\ \text{with value } a\,(1 + d)^{-1/d} \text{ and slope } ab\,(1 + d)^{-1/d - 1} \\
\text{Also written}: &\quad \text{logistic } (d = 1);\ \text{Gompertz } (d \to 0);\ \text{saturating exponential } (d = -1)
\end{aligned}
$$

The Richards function is a family of growth curves with an upper asymptote, in which a
fourth parameter sets how asymmetric the curve is. Richards (1959) proposed it as a
flexible function for the growth of plants, and it is used when neither the logistic nor
the Gompertz function describes the data well, for example for the growth of individual
plants (Damgaard et al. 2002). Its interest for this book is that it contains several of
the functions of this supplement as special cases (Haefner 1996; Damgaard et al. 2002),
so it shows how they are related. In general it is a phenomenological function, although
particular values of the shape parameter give functions that have a mechanism. Other
generalisations of the logistic function exist: Emlen (1996) raised $x$ to a power inside
the exponential, and Schnute (1981) proposed a growth function that is more general
still.

The function is

$$
f(x)=\frac{a}{\left[1+d\,e^{-b(x-c)}\right]^{1/d}},
$$

where $a$ is the upper asymptote, $b$ is a rate, $c$ is the location of the inflection
point and $d$ is the shape parameter. As for the [Gompertz](#sec-fn-gompertz) function we
write $u=e^{-b(x-c)}$, so that $f(x)=a\,(1+du)^{-1/d}$. As $x\to\infty$, $u\to0$ and
$f(x)\to a$. When $d>0$, $u$ grows without bound as $x\to-\infty$ and $f(x)\to0$. When $d$
is negative the term $1+du$ reaches zero at $u=-1/d$, so the function starts from zero at
$x=c+\log(-d)/b$ and is used from that value onwards.

The special cases follow from the value of $d$:

| Shape parameter | Function | Value at the inflection point |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $d=1$ | [Logistic](#sec-fn-logistic), $a/\left(1+e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | $a/2$ |
| $d\to0$ | [Gompertz](#sec-fn-gompertz), $a\exp\left(-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | $a/e\approx0.37\,a$ |
| $d=-1/3$ | Generalised [von Bertalanffy](#sec-fn-von-bertalanffy) with an exponent of 3 | $8a/27\approx0.30\,a$ |
| $d=-1$ | [Saturating exponential](#sec-fn-monomolecular), $a\left(1-e^{-b(x-c)}\right)$ | 0 (no inflection point) |

The cases $d=1$ and $d=-1$ are found by substituting the value in the formula. For the
Gompertz function we use the limit that defines the exponential function,
$(1+du)^{1/d}\to e^{u}$ as $d\to0$. For $d=-1/3$ the function is
$a\left(1-\tfrac{1}{3}u\right)^{3}$, and since $\tfrac{1}{3}e^{-b(x-c)}=e^{-b(x-c')}$ with
$c'=c-\log 3/b$, this is the generalised von Bertalanffy function that starts at $c'$.
Note that the parameters $a$, $b$ and $c$ keep their meaning along the whole family.

The chain rule, with $du/dx=-bu$, gives

$$
f'(x)=ab\,u\,(1+du)^{-1/d-1}=\frac{b}{d}\,f(x)\left[1-\left(\frac{f(x)}{a}\right)^{d}\right],
$$

where the last step uses $1+du=\left(a/f(x)\right)^{d}$. For $d=1$ this is the derivative
of the logistic function, $b\,f(x)\left(1-f(x)/a\right)$. Differentiating the last
expression once more with the product rule:

$$
f''(x)=\frac{b}{d}\,f'(x)\left[1-(1+d)\left(\frac{f(x)}{a}\right)^{d}\right].
$$

Since $f'(x)$ is positive, the second derivative is zero only where
$\left(f(x)/a\right)^{d}=1/(1+d)$. This happens where $1+du=1+d$, that is, where $u=1$ and
$x=c$. So for every $d>-1$ the inflection point is at $x=c$, and

$$
f(c)=a\,(1+d)^{-1/d}, \qquad f'(c)=ab\,(1+d)^{-1/d-1}.
$$

The shape parameter therefore decides at which fraction of the asymptote the function is
steepest: the fraction increases with $d$, from zero at $d=-1$ through one half at $d=1$
towards one for large $d$. As for the other exponents of this group, $d$ is hard to
estimate from data.

### Example: growth of an annual plant

Suppose that the dry mass of a plant (g) as a function of the time since emergence $x$
(days) follows a Richards function with $a=50$ g, $b=0.1$ per day, $c=30$ days and
$d=0.5$. The plant grows fastest at 30 days, when its mass is

$$
f(30)=50\times(1+0.5)^{-1/0.5}=\frac{50}{1.5^2}\approx22.2 \text{ g},
$$

that is, 44% of its final mass, and it then grows by
$ab\,(1+d)^{-1/d-1}=50\times0.1/1.5^3\approx1.48$ g per day. At emergence its mass is
$50/\left(1+0.5\,e^{3}\right)^{2}\approx0.41$ g, and after 60 days it is
$50/\left(1+0.5\,e^{-3}\right)^{2}\approx47.6$ g. With the same $a$, $b$ and $c$, a
logistic function would give 25 g at 30 days and a Gompertz function $50/e\approx18.4$ g.
We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Richards function: upper asymptote a, rate b, inflection point c and shape d
richards = function(x, a = 1, b = 1, c = 0, d = 1) {
  a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)
}

# Dry mass (g) at emergence, at 30 days and at 60 days
richards(x = c(0, 30, 60), a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.5)

# Slope at the inflection point: D() and the formula a * b * (1 + d)^(-1 / d - 1)
richards_derivative = D(expression(a / (1 + d * exp(-b * (x - c)))^(1 / d)), "x")
eval(richards_derivative, list(a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.5, x = 30))
50 * 0.1 * (1 + 0.5)^(-1 / 0.5 - 1)

# The second derivative is zero (up to rounding error) at the inflection point
eval(D(richards_derivative, "x"), list(a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.5, x = 30))

# Special cases at 10, 30 and 45 days: d = 1 is the logistic function
days = c(10, 30, 45)
richards(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 1)
logistic(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30)

# A shape parameter close to 0 gives the Gompertz function
richards(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.000001)
gompertz(x = days, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30)

# d = -1 is the saturating exponential function that starts at c (here from 30 days)
richards(x = c(30, 45, 60), a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = -1)
saturating_exponential(x = c(30, 45, 60) - 30, a = 50, b = 0.1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Richards functions with a = 50, b = 0.1 and c = 30, for a shape parameter d close to 0 (dotted line; a Gompertz function), d = 1 (dashed line; a logistic function) and d = 4 (solid line). The dashed grey line marks the inflection point, which is at x = c for the three functions; the value of the function there increases with d."
x_values = seq(-20, 100, length.out = 500)
curve_data = data.frame(
  x = rep(x_values, times = 3),
  y = c(richards(x_values, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 4),
        richards(x_values, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 1),
        richards(x_values, a = 50, b = 0.1, c = 30, d = 0.000001)),
  curve = rep(c("d = 4", "d = 1", "d close to 0"), each = length(x_values))
)
curve_data$curve = factor(curve_data$curve, levels = c("d = 4", "d = 1", "d close to 0"))

ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = x, y = y, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 30, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: the shape parameter and the inflection point"}

The number of breeding pairs in a colony of seabirds follows a Richards function with $a=200$
pairs, $b=0.3$ per year, $c=10$ years and $d=2$. How large is the colony when it grows
fastest, as a number of pairs and as a fraction of its final size? How fast does it grow
then? Compare the fraction with that of a logistic function.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The colony grows fastest at the inflection point, $x=c=10$ years. Its size is then
$a\,(1+d)^{-1/d}=200\times3^{-1/2}\approx115$ pairs, a fraction $3^{-1/2}\approx0.58$ of
its final size, and it grows by $ab\,(1+d)^{-1/d-1}=200\times0.3\times3^{-3/2}\approx11.5$
pairs per year. A logistic function ($d=1$) is steepest at half of its asymptote, so with
$d=2$ the fastest growth comes later in the approach to the asymptote.

:::
::::

# Functions without a closed form {#sec-fn-no-closed-form}

Every function of this supplement is given by a formula: for any value of $x$ and of the
parameters we can calculate $f(x)$ directly. Such a formula is called a closed form. Some
functions that are used in ecology are defined by an equation that $f(x)$ has to satisfy,
and for some of these equations no formula for the solution exists in terms of the
functions that we have used here. The value of the function then has to be calculated
numerically for each value of $x$, for example by finding a root with `uniroot()`. This
book does not use such functions, so we only name the two that are met most often.

The **Rogers random-predator equation** describes the number of prey that a predator eats
during an experiment in which the prey that have been eaten are not replaced, so that
their density declines while the experiment runs (Rogers 1972; Juliano 1993). It starts
from the same assumptions as the
[disc equation](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd#sec-mechanistic), but the number of prey eaten
appears on both sides of the resulting equation and cannot be isolated. Its solution can
be written with a special function, the Lambert W function (Corless et al. 1996).

The **theta-logistic model** generalises the model of population growth that leads to the
[logistic](#sec-fn-logistic) function: the growth rate per individual declines with the
density of the population raised to a power $\theta$ (Nelder 1961; Richards 1959; Thomas
et al. 1980; Sibly et al. 2005). It is defined by an equation for the growth rate of the
population, it is usually solved numerically, and it is often listed among the functions
without a closed form. It does have one: the derivative of the
[Richards](#sec-fn-richards) function,
$f'(x)=(b/d)\,f(x)\left[1-(f(x)/a)^{d}\right]$, is this model with a carrying capacity
$a$, a growth rate $b/d$ and an exponent $\theta=d$, so the Richards function is its
solution.
